en: Regarding the "Hanging Instructions on the Correct Pulse of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa*":

those who provide old interpretations merely know to admire the perfect subtlety of the sūtra, yet they are unable to follow the scriptural text closely to investigate deeply its inherently possessed, perfectly subtle meaning.
Instead, they cite meanings from other schools that vaguely resemble this perfect subtlety to attempt a harmonious explanation; therefore, [this work is undertaken].

However, the words and meanings therein do not accord at all; moreover, they have caused the original structural continuity of this sutra to become entirely disordered, such that the beginning and end do not cohere.
Therefore, in this new commentary, I shall simply follow the Buddha’s sutra and thoroughly investigate its fundamental intent.
This causes the channels and vessels to penetrate one another; thus, the inherently perfect, wondrous, and profound meaning within the sutra cannot be compared to that of other schools.

This is why it is called the "Correct Pulse" (Zhengmai); this is the intended meaning. However, the structural divisions and interpretive principles within this commentary differ greatly from previous explanations.

Fearing that those who hear them might suddenly become startled or suspicious, or perhaps give rise to derision, I have therefore provided a preliminary overview before the actual exegesis of the sutra.

I shall set forth its essential meanings to guide people toward joyful appreciation, so that it does not fall into neglect or abandonment. This work consists of two sections: first, an exposition of the grounds for my own interpretation;
second, a presentation of the structural framework according to ancient models. Now, regarding the first—my exposition of the grounds for my interpretation:

since this sutra began circulating in China during the Tang dynasty until the present day, more than a thousand years have passed. Those who have grasped its principles and expressed them in literary form are indeed...
They are beyond reckoning; yet the collections of works by renowned masters nearly fill a dozen volumes.

Tianru selected the writings of nine such masters, synthesizing them through a process of inclusion and exclusion, and supplemented them with his own insights, titling the work *The Collected Explanations of the Ten Masters*. He claimed that it possessed all manner of excellence.

Thus, he severed all hesitation; his exposition of the meaning was exhaustive, leaving nothing unclarified. People were moved to admiration for its comprehensiveness and breadth, yet they also delighted in its conciseness and essentiality, as it struck the vital point of the times.

Consequently, they praised his excellence with one voice and vied with one another to study and discuss his work. From the end of the Yuan dynasty until the present day, [it has remained influential].

For over two hundred years, among those within the realm who have admired the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and engaged in its study and exposition, they have known only the *Huìjiě* (Commentary on the Essential Meaning), and nothing else has been held in high esteem.
Therefore, those seeking the purport of the scripture must derive their explanations from within the *Huìjiě*; as for anything that cannot be reconciled with it, [it is disregarded].
Consequently, they place the blame on the scriptures for being profound and difficult to clarify, rarely daring to suspect that the commentators have not fully mastered them.
Should there be those who raise even slight doubts or criticisms, they are met with a torrent of slander as if they were rebels;

this is because of long-standing habits and the prevailing sentiments of the masses, so it is no cause for wonder. If this is the case, then although there are already many expositors, [the situation remains as follows:]...
The assembly has already reached a consensus; those who follow it are numerous and chaotic, so there should be no further need for explanation.
That I have now once again provided this explanation must surely have another reason. If I do not state it at the outset, how can I guide others to advance toward its study?

Furthermore, I shall divide it into four parts: first, the beginning and end of the commentary (*śāstra*); second, a brief refutation of doubts and arrogance; third, a comparative analysis of merits and faults; fourth...

I shall briefly analyze right and wrong. Regarding the initial composition of this commentary from beginning to end: In my youth, I followed the Confucian path and did not know what the Buddha-dharma was.

At times, I even harbored slanderous views toward it. However, when Master Xianglin, my own secular teacher, alerted me to the writings of Yongjia, I suddenly recognized the Tathāgata as the parents of my long-lost consciousness.
I felt profound remorse and immediately vowed to leave the household life; yet, I had not yet...
There was a profound understanding [of this]. Not long after, I entered the Imperial Academy to serve as a member of the staff.

While seeking out the Buddhist scriptures (Zhudi), I encountered my friend, the layman Guo Xiyu, who bestowed upon me this commentary. It was like obtaining a *maṇi* jewel without having crossed the ocean; my joy was immeasurable.
Amidst it all, there were moments of vague realization where I gained some insight, yet I truly had not yet attained full mastery. At that time, I visited Master Wuwen at Qingta Temple.

While seated beneath [the master], the scope of our discussions extended to the lecture halls of various masters, including Master Xiān and others, as well as my fellow practitioners. Together we deliberated and reached a refined consensus;
my appreciation for the teachings grew ever deeper, and my delight in them was insatiable. I came to grasp, to some extent, the principle that "the myriad dharmas are but mind.
Nevertheless, my wisdom and insight remained largely confined to the commentaries and sub-commentaries, and I did not dare to transcend them. From this point on, I began to explore other avenues...
Regarding the various scriptures on nature and characteristics (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*), he roamed freely through the meanings and phrases of the *Lotus Sūtra*.

Having fully satiated himself with the joy of the Tiantai patriarchs' school through the commentaries and sub-commentaries of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, both its texts and meanings were thoroughly mastered without the slightest difficulty.

As the light of his mind gradually dawned, he looked back upon [Zhi]hui’s *Huayan jieshe* and realized that its insights were incomplete and its speculative assertions were largely unrestrained, being quite inconsistent with the established traditions of those two great masters.
It was as if, when he applied himself to Confucian studies, his mind grew weary, yet when he confronted the Buddhist scriptures, his spirit became clear.

With a focused mind and settled will, he dreamed of leaving the household life and being born in the Pure Land more than ten times a month. Suddenly, however, he encountered the decay and loss of his own kin.
He had undergone numerous instances of mourning and funeral rites, even reaching the point of observing the period of intense grief for his mother.

At that time, a lay practitioner surnamed Zhou invited him to spend the summer retreat at Zhenguosi Temple, where he lectured on the Four Books alongside various eminent monks. This was during the era of the ancient style of Changde, when the Venerable Gufeng emerged from the lineage of the Single Transmission (Danyuan).
Sifafa Xiaoshan was well-versed in the fundamental tenets of the school, yet he had not yet emerged into the world to teach others.

Consequently, [the Master] compelled him to engage in a formal exchange of views, discussing them repeatedly until they could together immerse themselves in the *gong'an* verses of the four masters and the commentaries of the three patriarchs.

Thereupon, his mind became suddenly expansive; words were forgotten and thought ceased. In that very moment, all was as it is—his heart was empty and serene, such that mountains, rivers, and people were all seen as they truly are.
Yingxiang went one day to the eastern study of the former official Cao Gong’s residence within the city.
Happening upon it being unoccupied, he composed his mind and sat in stillness for some time. Seeing a volume of commentaries on the *Huayan jing* on a shelf, he took it up and examined it;
he did not know what state of realization this was, but suddenly his vision became clear and lucid and the chambers of his mind opened wide regarding that which the Tathāgata had taught.
It winds and turns in every direction, leaving nothing unseen.

It is like being in a great mansion on an ordinary day, where dark chambers, shadowy rooms, winding alleys, and twisting corridors make it impossible to distinguish east from west or clarify what lies before or behind;
yet now, as if suddenly ascending the highest terrace, one can see every detail and intricacy therein with complete clarity. (As stated in various commentaries:)
The errors in the original scripture were like measuring the straightness of a curve with a plumb line and a carpenter’s square; not even a fraction of an inch could be concealed.
Thereupon, with a mixture of sorrow and joy, he approached the scripture and prostrated himself, as if personally facing the Tathāgata.

His body hair stood on end as he made a vow to eventually leave the household life, praying for a long life to annotate the scripture and leave it behind for the world. After several days, he encountered Han Zixi, a student at the school in Lu'an.
In the past, he had been a fervent admirer of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* for twenty years, traveling extensively to consult various lecturers, yet none could satisfy his mind.

He eventually came before me and presented several difficult points of inquiry, all of which I resolved with thorough explanations. Han was already impressed by this; however, when I turned the questioning back upon him, Han became utterly bewildered and failed to understand, unable to offer a single word in response.
He was then greatly struck with awe and admiration, bowing and requesting that I provide provisions so that we might plan to stay together, wishing to prolong our time together.

Because he had thoroughly investigated the subtle and profound, I knew that this great family possessed the Taihang Mountains, where a Zen hermitage could provide a place for quiet dwelling so that he might fulfill his aspiration to leave the household life.
Regarding the matter of annotating the scriptures, I immediately expressed my intention and asked him to first return and wait for me. Han was overcome with joy and gratitude.
The following year, I arrived as agreed upon, and he immediately shaved his head. He vowed to study the teachings for ten years to sharpen his faculties. At that time...

It was the tenth month of winter in the fourth year of the Wanli era, the year of Bingzi. Following the questions and answers with Master Han, I completed the four-fascicle *Lengyan Tonghui* (Comprehensive Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra).
This manuscript copy has not yet been published; its composition resulted from extensive study of the teachings. Four years passed without my being able to travel south.
Upon returning, I resided at Beidong Town for another two years, where I was invited by Li Tongfu, Duke Jingshan, to reside at Fazhu Temple and establish the Huazang (Flower-Treasury) assembly.
I resided in the upper chamber. Another four years passed; I reflected that the ten-year agreement had already been fulfilled, yet I had still not composed commentaries.
While I was hesitating, many in the monastery fell ill and became uneasy. I made a vow, saying, "May my own person take their place. Immediately thereafter, I fell ill.
After more than half a month, I was on the verge of death. My relatives gathered around me as I lay in a state of stupor, when I felt someone seize my arm and warn me, saying:
"The Buddha has come! Startled, I rose and knelt facing west. Looking up at the one who had alerted me, it was Avalokiteśvara.
I saw the Buddha standing in the center with two Great Beings flanking him on either side; all were golden in color, their radiance brilliant and clear, each extending for more than a zhang.

I immediately realized they had come to welcome me to the Pure Land. I cried out, "The supreme aspiration is rebirth [in the Pure Land]! Alas, the old commentaries on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* are so disordered and confused!

I had not yet written a commentary on it. I heard the Buddha’s resonant voice say, "Truly, it is disordered. As soon as he finished speaking, I saw the Three Sages all turn their bodies and depart toward the west.
I gazed after them, seeing the golden backs and the blue-spiraled hair at the nape of their necks; they grew faint and gradually receded into the distance.
When I opened my eyes, my body was dripping with sweat like rain. Everyone asked me how I was and comforted me, and I related in detail what I had seen, saying further: "I..."
"I have already granted you leave to annotate the sutras; for now, you shall not die. You need not worry. The assembly all recited the Buddha's name, their voices shaking the very buildings.

This was in the sixth month of summer in the *wanzhi* year of Bingxu. Subsequently, my condition gradually recovered, and the members of the monastery indeed felt themselves suddenly at ease from the time I fell ill in my quarters.
Moved by this auspicious sign, I was deeply awakened. By the tenth month of winter, I performed repentance rites and prayed to Avalokiteśvara.
He bestowed his spiritual protection and subsequently took up the brush to annotate the scriptures. By the end of that year, the annotations were completed.
In the spring of the following year, Prince An-gyeong invited him to reside at Bogeun Hall in the southwestern corner of the city, where he stayed for ten years.

During this time, he did not engage in any worldly affairs or internal or external lecture periods; yet, his work on the commentaries continued day and night without the slightest interruption until the *Wanli* cycle’s *Bingchen* year.

In the winter of the [year] *shen*, the commentary was completed. In the second month of spring in the following year, *dingyou*, the Prince of the Shen Prefecture ordered that monks be fed at Mount Luya on Mount Wutai;
consequently, I spent the summer retreat at Luya and composed this *xuānpàn* (suspended judgment).
Thus, I record the date and time to show the beginning and end of the composition of this commentary.

Second, regarding the brief refutation of doubt and pride: it is not that I dare to seek the respect and faith of others. Rather, it is because the three doubts linger in my thoughts and the seven types of pride dwell in my mind;
these are most capable of obstructing a person’s open-mindedness and hindering their reception of the good. It is for this reason that I have composed this commentary.

They will certainly be unable to rejoice in, view, or accept [this work], and may instead give rise to separate criticisms. How could such things accomplish the benefit of establishing a karmic connection?
Therefore, I have briefly refuted them merely to encourage those who would rejoice. When I was composing these commentaries, much time had passed;

it was difficult to exhaustively address all hidden rumors and hearsay, and those who slandered me were beyond counting. There were even those who confronted me face-to-face and rebuked me. A brief account of this follows:

He said: "This sutra has already been interpreted by the ancients; many scholars who have attained awakening are great men capable of universal salvation. Their words follow from evidence, and their principles arise from within their own hearts.
Thus it is said: 'Should there be later authors, none could possibly surpass them. Who are you to dare to affirm or deny the ancients?
It is like someone who has only just taken up an axe and immediately laughs at Gongshu Ban, or a novice who has barely tuned his strings and suddenly attempts to outshine Shi Kang."
"How could you avoid the laughter of the wise? Yet, as a student of the final age, you do not follow [the sages]; this will surely lead to inexhaustible shame. I pray that you follow my words;
it would be better for you to cease [your objections] immediately. I replied slowly: "The ancients have provided exhaustive explanations;

those who come after should simply adhere to them and must not attempt further interpretation. This is truly the ultimate teaching, and I shall offer my thanks for it. However, I venture to ask one question in response."
"Does the Elder mean that the ten schools within the *Huìjiě* (Comprehensive Commentary) all emerged at one time?
Or were there earlier and later periods? He replied, "They succeeded one another across generations, spanning a thousand years; how can they be called 'one time'?

I said, "If there were indeed earlier and later periods, then the first school to provide an interpretation must have been an ancient one. In that case, their interpretations should have been exhausted [by now], yet..."
Regarding these two schools: when it comes to the time of the latter interpretation, they are entirely people of the present day who laugh at the ancients for not having fully explained [the text].
If this were so, then the Venerable Zhiyi should have censured them as students of the final age and their deviations from the truth; why then do they both proceed together without contradiction?

How much more so regarding the interpretations of the ten schools today, all of which proceed in parallel? Why, moreover, do you conversely claim that only the final "Comprehensive Explanation" (Huìjiě) is unique?
Excellent! In the past, Qingliang remarked that the Sage’s intent is profound and far-reaching, and that it comprehensively precludes these difficulties.

You have simply not yet investigated his text. This is because the meaning of the Dharma is inexhaustible and the Buddha’s words are exceedingly deep. If a single person were to exhaustively understand them, how could one say that the Dharma is inexhaustible and the words are exceedingly deep?
He cited the individual explanations of the causes of the body, which the Buddha permitted as being without difference; this is based on the Perfect [Teaching].
Regarding the various alternative formulations (*paryāya*), the Buddha’s clarity does not differentiate between them.

By inferring from this sense of unimpededness (*anāvaraṇa*), even if a hundred treatises were presented side by side, what hindrance would there be to illuminating the gift of the Dharma together according to one's own insight? You need only investigate the merits and defects of their meanings and examine whether their principles are correct or incorrect;
you should not reject them simply because they have already been explained by ancients. He further attempts to defend [his position], saying: "All..."

Although various commentaries have appeared in succession, their divergent interpretations are manifold and their validity remains unsettled; thus, they might have been permitted for comparative synthesis.
However, Tianru has already compiled these various theories and distinguished between them, making his selections precise and appropriate so that the definitive argument is established.

Moreover, this school has long been practiced and studied until it is settled beyond doubt. Why, then, should one again create such confusion and disturb the minds of people? [This response was written by Changshui.]
Regarding the *Yihai* (Ocean of Meaning), there have already been commentaries by several masters prior to this.

Yet, why did Changshui name his work the *Yihai*, unless he considered himself to have gathered the various streams and synthesized their essential points? Furthermore, the metaphor of the "ocean" signifies that all meanings are fully complete with nothing further remaining.
Moreover, since this work has long been included in the Tripitaka, who would not have studied it? Why, then, would later generations [seek another commentary]?
Is it only when there is a *Huìjiě* (Comprehensive Commentary) that it can be considered a definitive treatise? This *Yìhǎi* (Ocean of Meanings) does not necessarily encompass every meaning.

Indeed, the *Huìjiě* itself did not consider the *Yìhǎi* sufficient, yet it still dared to provide further explanations. Now, why do you hastily regard the *Huìjiě* as sufficient and dare not provide further explanations?
Furthermore, you claim that others have already mastered the fixed [text] and are settled and free from doubt; yet, as for yourself—
I shall merely mention this. Previously, I already offered my limited observations by pointing out several errors and criticizing them; these have already become widely circulated.
Recently, I heard that there is one known as Master Sanhuai in the Southern Capital who criticizes [the *Huayan jing shuchao*] even more severely.

In his lectures, he never follows the *Huayan jing shuchao* at all, but speaks only from the original text. Not everyone disagrees with him, yet those who follow him are numerous. Furthermore, I have heard that there is someone in Suzhou...
The title of this work is unknown. It extensively refutes the errors of various commentaries; it has already been published, yet it has not seen widespread circulation.

Others, such as *Gekkan no bettan* (The Moon River’s Special Eye) and *Chōin no kenkyō* (Chōin’s Hanging Mirror), all present their own individual views rather than being restricted to the *Kaige* (Combined Explanations).
However, these are merely partial and independent assertions that have not based themselves upon the full text to fundamentally overturn previous cases. Recently, too...
There are gentlemen who revere the inner teaching and possess the eye of wisdom; they often cherish the unsurpassed nature of the sūtras yet lament that the commentaries are not yet perfect.
This is sufficient proof that the profound and far-reaching, tranquil meaning of the Buddha-dharma is difficult to exhaust;
how could it be fully revealed by a single commentary? Your own intelligence falls short of such a commentary and lacks transcendent insight; how could it possibly [suffice]?
"Can one force everyone to be like you? He replied with even greater indignation and displeasure: "The authors of ancient works all possessed realization and verification;
some were originally from the ranks of the sages, and thus it is fitting to follow them. Now, you are but a single ordinary person with no extraordinary conduct or reputation to speak of.
It is not necessarily the case that there are none among us who do not satisfy the hearts of men, yet you disregard this and think nothing of it."
"I will never believe what you say regarding this matter. I replied, "Even though the Buddha is the most holy being, he cannot cause everyone to believe him;
there are countless people in his own time who spread slander. How much more so for those in different times and different places? If you still do not believe me,"

"Leave it to them; let them not believe. To claim that I am not a sage because I lack extraordinary conduct, and furthermore, that I do not fully satisfy the expectations of people's minds—these few words are not sufficient grounds for debate.

Do you perhaps suggest that all the sages and wise ones of antiquity maintained a dualistic view of 'sage' and 'ordinary person,' and that they too necessarily performed manifest acts of eccentricity to startle and move the world? Moreover, the Buddha [taught] by means of the four sages..."
These are words of ultimate truth. Not only does it state that all people shall become Buddhas, but it further clarifies that sentient beings are fundamentally Buddhas from the very beginning.
To those who are unable to believe and accept this, it is said: "People of meager virtue and little merit do not trust themselves to become Buddhas.

Therefore, within the lineage of the Patriarchs, there was concern that people would over-exalt the sacred realm while disparaging themselves and retreating in discouragement; thus, they exerted every effort [to remedy this].
They eradicate these evil views, repeatedly disparaging the ancients and exalting the present. Uttering a single phrase offhand, they claim it to be discourse that transcends Buddhas and patriarchs;
their intent is that the emotions of the holy and the mundane are exhausted, and demons and Buddhas are one and the same. They even go so far as to revile the Buddhas and curse the patriarchs.
How could one help but do so? It is simply because every person is shrouded by the views of the holy and the ordinary; being biased, base, vulgar, and weak, they lack the spirit of a true man.
How, then, could they bear the burden of the work of the patriarchs and Buddhas? Therefore, this extraordinary and vigorous exhortation was made.
Thus, even a man of noble character should first have confidence that he is a Buddha and act as a Buddha, following the words of the Buddha to bring forth [his realization].
Regarding the fundamental intent of the sutras, why should I feel deficient for not possessing the "sage-like" [eccentric] conduct? You further doubt that I lack such extraordinary practices;
yet how do you know that when Oxhead and Mazu had not yet attained awakening, each displayed distinct eccentricities, whereas after their awakening, none failed to change their ways?

Thus one knows that it is not necessary to seek [the truth] within eccentric conduct. The entire ancestral gate values plainness and reality above all else: eating when hungry and sleeping when weary—this is it.
This refers to the profound and subtle. Carrying water and hauling firewood are all considered wondrous functions.

Furthermore, Jiufeng said that although Zhiyi’s śarīra were countless, they were not equal to having uttered a single phrase of the Way at that time. Huangbo saw the supernatural powers of an Arhat and regretted not having broken his leg.
The ancients valued only the penetration of wisdom into Prajñā; those who dwelt upon eccentric practices and supernatural powers were considered commoners.
This is how it is seen. Furthermore, the roots of goodness of sentient beings are all unfathomable. The Patriarch, wishing to warn people against doubt and arrogance, also said:
"I have already practiced through many kalpas; this is not a casual deception. You do not possess the supernormal powers of past-life recollection.
This merely resembles the perceived deeds of people in their present lives; how could one know of the cultivation performed by others over billions of kalpas?
The Tathāgata’s golden mouth personally declared that those who believe in the Prajñāpāramitā have already planted various roots of goodness under hundreds of thousands of Buddhas.

How much more so for this sutra, the supreme essence of the finest cream (*amṛta*); those who can believe and understand it shall illuminate it together with the multitude. How could I dare to disparage myself?
If you cannot believe in yourself or believe in others, you will ultimately end up insulting others and insulting yourself; this is truly a great pity.

Furthermore, the right and wrong of human affairs are difficult to determine, and the truth or falsehood of people’s words has no basis for verification. This is the legacy of the Patriarchs dwelling in the world.

Driven by shifting circumstances, one cannot escape being judged as right or wrong; consequently, one often encounters censure and punishment from the era, as seen in the cases of Miaoxi, Shimen, and others—such instances are innumerable.
How could they have fully satisfied the hearts of the people of that time? Judging by this, we may evaluate the matter accordingly.
Thus, your words cannot be considered reasonable. Generally speaking, such is the constant nature of the corruptions in this Sahā world.
Now, you single out the ancients for special honor merely because they were not born at the same time as you. Had you been their contemporaries...
"In that case, there would be no difference from today; how could you possibly escape my suspicion and disdain?
The third point was to compare and explain merits and faults. Upon hearing these words, the man’s expression finally settled; he apologized to me with shame, saying:

"Having received your instruction, not only will I no longer harbor suspicion or disdain toward you, but I shall also cease to doubt or feel disdainful of myself. However, I have one thought that I have been privately harboring..."

I am not yet satisfied; I beg you to further elaborate upon this. Generally speaking, when it comes to writing commentaries, it is easy for those who follow established works, but difficult for those who initiate them.
The various masters initiated the composition of these commentaries, and I have relied upon their resources to clarify the meaning of the sutras; my debt of gratitude toward them is no small matter.

I have heard that you, sir, have also spent ten years immersing yourself in the sub-commentaries before finally developing your own distinct insights. Thus, you too have been indebted to these masters.
"Their grace was not shallow. Now, if you were to suddenly act contrary to this, exalting your own wisdom to obscure the excellence of your teachers—would you truly bear to do such a thing?
I clapped my hands and laughed, saying: "You understand the small, but have not yet clarified the great.
Furthermore, as for these two claims—that one should 'exalt one's own wisdom' and 'obscure the excellence of one's teachers'—both are incorrect. You have merely been moved by your teachers..."

While possessing the virtue of having been inspired [to study], one remains shrouded in ignorance and delusion; yet one never considers the immeasurable grace of the Tathāgata over incalculable *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, which must necessarily be repaid.
One should not allow various teachers to act as obstacles, thereby avoiding transgression out of fear.

Therefore, whenever I have found even a fleeting moment of clarity to glimpse the Buddhist scriptures, I have encountered cases where their wondrous purport was either obscured or hidden, or where they were fragmented and distorted.
To lose its original intent would cause me unrest day and night, and I would feel ashamed before the Buddha’s grace.

Whenever anything deviates from the purport of the Buddha-dharma, it severs the lineage of the Way and misleads sentient beings; how could I bear to sit idly by without making a formal representation to clarify and rectify it?
How else could I repay the Buddha’s supreme kindness? My reflections rest solely upon this; it is not that I wish to boast of my own meager wisdom. Furthermore, you said:
To say that this conceals the virtues of the various masters is even more incorrect.

When I composed my commentary, if there was even a hair’s breadth of merit in the works of the various masters, I clearly indicated their names and titles in the *Huìjiě* (Comprehensive Explanation) and recorded them directly; I never secretly appropriated them as my own.

Where something was inappropriate, I simply omitted it and did not mention it again—this is not concealing their virtues, but rather [avoiding what is unsound]. To claim otherwise is to obscure the truth.
Regarding their right and wrong, they shall no longer be subject to the censure of the wise.

Should there occasionally be that which appears correct but is actually false, or where one fears people cannot resolve what to adopt or reject, or where matters concern the Great Meaning such that one has no choice but to provide clarification, I shall merely substitute the two characters of the old commentary for the person's name, not wishing to identify them by person. Were it not so, [the work] would ultimately...
This would be to obscure the Buddha’s intent and to suppress the meaning of the sutras. You cannot bear to conceal the excellence of the former masters;

how could you bear to obscure the wondrous teachings of the Tathāgata? You should know that while the fault of contradicting the commentaries of the former masters is shallow, the fault of obscuring the intent and meaning of the Tathāgata is profound.
The error is profound indeed; for it obstructs the eye of wisdom of sentient beings, blocks the gate of enlightenment for learners, and utterly辜负 (betrays) the grace of the Buddha.
Furthermore, to merely protect the commentaries of various masters is of little merit; rather, one should elucidate the original intent of the Tathāgata.
The merit of this is great; for by immediately opening the eye of wisdom and unlocking the gate of enlightenment, one truly repays the Buddha’s kindness.
Furthermore, when a teacher nurtures his disciples, how could he wish their wisdom to remain entirely inferior to his own? Were such a mind to exist, it would be nothing but a source of affliction.

Such a person is not a true enlightened teacher and is not worthy of veneration. Therefore, the Chan school says: "If the son does not equal his father, the family lineage will decline for a generation.

Furthermore, when a father hears that his son is capable, he regrets not having sacrificed himself [for the Dharma]. This is entirely because their minds are impartial in their dedication to the Dharma.

Yet I do not act out of self-interest to promote my own reputation. Although I have only recently read the *Huìjiě* (Commentary on the Compendium), and even among these various masters there exists the distinction between teacher and disciple, I am able to cause what has been transmitted to flourish and to complete their unfinished legacy.
While one who acts in accordance with benevolence does not yield, I have briefly adjudicated right and wrong at this single moment;
in doing so, I truly rectify the errors of the past without fault, ensuring that flaws shall be forever extinguished for a hundred generations. How could this be [the work] of those other masters?

Originally, all were eminent worthies who served the Dharma with sincere hearts. How could it be that they would merely seek private fame for themselves, while conversely disliking the glorification of the Dharma?
It is on this basis that I have confidence; the various masters will surely not reproach me too severely.
Thus, I have drafted this commentary. What do you think of it?
The fourth point, "Briefly Distinguishing Right from Wrong," states: Upon reaching this stage, the person is struck with alarm and says:

"How could the Tathāgata’s original intent and sublime purport tolerate even a hair’s breadth of concealment or distortion? How can the gate of awakening for the wisdom-eye of sentient beings remain unclosed for even a single day?
It was only because of my own lack of acuity that, despite long-term study and repeated listening, I failed to realize there were such deficiencies. Yet now I have heard your words..."
I have composed a commentary, yet I truly did not believe it could further clarify the meaning. Now, having received this [work] you have shown me, I am truly struck with great alarm and trepidation.
I fear it may not necessarily be so. Your commentary follows the text closely and is so extensive that I fear it cannot be fully grasped at once.

I venture to request that you briefly indicate the general outline and distinguish one or two points of success and failure, so that I may first gain conviction and only then proceed to master the entire commentary.
Having received this question, I folded my sleeves and concentrated my spirit for a long while. Then, sighing deeply, I said: "How difficult it is to speak of this!

Formerly, when Qingliang [Fazang] composed his commentary on the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, he also expressed the difficulty of speaking of it, stating in brief: 'If suchness and phenomena were not blended and identical...'"

For he explicitly stated that if *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are taken in isolation—like a single wing or a solitary wheel—one cannot travel far.

Even if one were to seize upon one or two passages that appear similar and force them into alignment with this claim, it would be utterly devoid of rational meaning.

Furthermore, since these two types of cultivation—shallow and deep—are distinguished, a beginner must first practice the Perfect Penetration (*yuan-tong*) and subsequently practice the Three Contemplations (*san-guan*).

I venture to ask: at what stage of the path does one who cultivates *yuan-tong* (perfect penetration) first possess a profound mind (*shen-xin*), such that they may then cultivate the three contemplations (*san-guan*)?

According to the Bodhisattva’s own account, from his initial entry into the stream (*ru-liu*) up until the manifestation of cessation (*ji-mie-xian-qian*), there is no sign whatsoever of him practicing the three contemplations in succession.
Yet the Tathāgata states that "this faculty is first understood, whereby one first attains the emptiness of persons (*ren-kong*). According to the stages of the path, this corresponds to...

Reaching the seventh stage of faith (*śraddhā*), one is equal to a Lesser Arhat (*śrāvaka-arhat*). The Bodhisattva, for whom "that which is heard has been exhausted," seems to correspond to this stage.

Furthermore, it is said that when the "emptiness-nature" (*śūnyatā*) becomes perfectly luminous, one achieves the liberation of dharmas (*dharmavimukti*); according to the stages, this should correspond to the eighth or ninth stages of faith, having already transcended the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) of the Lesser Vehicle.
The Bodhisattva, for whom "that which empties emptiness is extinguished," seems to correspond to this stage. Again, it is said that when liberation and dharmas are both complete...
"Emptiness is non-arising. According to the stages, this should correspond to the fulfillment of the tenth stage of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*).

Is this not, then, already the stage of the Deep Mind (*gambhīra-citta*)? Why is there no mention of "connecting to the cultivation of the three contemplations" (*tri-vipaśyanā*) here either? Could it be that one only begins to cultivate them in a subsequent stage?

Yes. However, at this stage, the Bodhisattva has already transcended both the mundane and supramundane realms and gives rise to the boundless, wondrous functions of the three categories [of phenomena].
How could it be that the Three Contemplations (*sanguan*) taught by Tiantai are not yet capable of being cultivated by such Bodhisattvas?
Are those who practice the Three Contemplations today all Bodhisattvas of the First Abode (*prathamabhūmi*) and above? This is a great misunderstanding. The interlocutor offers this defense:

That which is called "universal" (tong) refers to that which can be practiced throughout the ten directions. That which is called "particular" (bie) refers to that which specifically addresses the capacities of beings in this direction.
The answer is: while all other gates universally address the capacities of beings in the ten directions, Mañjuśrī fully understands them and instructs people to abandon them;

the gate of the ear alone specifically addresses the capacities of beings in this direction, and Mañjuśrī uniquely selects it, instructing people to adopt it. Now, regarding the three contemplations (san guan)...

If this were a method for universal practice throughout the ten directions, rather than a teaching specifically suited to the capacities of those in this region, it would fall under the category of what Mañjuśrī excluded—something that should be abandoned and not cultivated.
Furthermore, why would the Tathāgata, at the very outset, provide a detailed exposition of a method that is unsuited to the needs of his audience?
This, too, is untenable. Moreover, as for the defense that "what he spoke of was universal," it is not so.
It penetrates other worlds, or it may penetrate only this Sahā world. Those at deep or shallow stages can all practice it;
as for the mention of "distinctive," this refers only to those at the initial stage. The answer is: if one follows the perspective of this region, regarding penetration, it remains the ear-door.
This is because the Tathāgata secretly pointed to the faculty of hearing as the single path to Nirvāṇa for the Bhagavans of the ten directions.
Mañjuśrī clearly selects the gateway of the ear, also saying that this is the single path to nirvāṇa for the Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust.

Below, he further reveals the method of universal cultivation practiced by the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time. Furthermore, he distinguishes it from other gateways, stating: "This is not a practice to be cultivated and studied [only] at certain times."

Since the Dharma is preached equally to those of shallow and deep capacities, this reflects that the gateway of the ears is a method accessible for cultivation by all, a gateway employed equally by both the shallow and the deep.
Who would say that perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*) is restricted only to the shallow stages and not a practice for the deep stages?

Furthermore, since the three contemplations (*sanguan*) are accessible for cultivation even at the shallow stages, they serve as skillful means (*upāya*) for beginners; why then must one point specifically toward [the ear-gate]?
Regarding the Ear Gate (*karṇadvāra*): Furthermore, the Ear Gate is a method for practicing both the shallow and the deep; this is clearly stated in the sutras.
Since the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) apply to both the shallow and the deep, what textual evidence from the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* can be cited [to the contrary]?

One should know that those who mistake fixed cessation (*śamatha*) for the nature of delusion, and who disparage the Perfect Penetration (*pariśuddha-prativedha*) as a shallow practice, all take such judgments as the root of their delusion. This must be thoroughly scrutinized and corrected.
Wash it away. Yet, there are still two kinds of things that remain undifferentiated: first, the failure to distinguish between the explanation of principle and the explanation of practice.

This is because the Tathāgata destroyed the deluded mind to point toward wondrous vision; he clarified that the nature is eternally abiding through the four categories; and he revealed that the nature is all-pervasive and perfect through the seven elements.
Furthermore, the ten delusions are the fundamental emptiness of the three continuities; the four meanings and four marks are the original subtlety.

Thus, even up to the full manifestation of the Three Baskets (Tripitaka), all of these merely discuss the wondrous principle inherently possessed by my own mind; they truly have not yet reached the opening of the gates of practice or the establishment of the methods of contemplation.
Why, then, do various commentaries compete to judge the three types of cessation-and-contemplation? That being the case, as for the rational nature and—

Even regarding contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), there is as yet no clear discernment; how then can one hope for it to manifest the profound intent of the sutras? Second, there is no distinction between awakening through the teaching and cultivation through the teaching.

This is because, generally speaking, when the fundamental nature is not clarified and realization has not yet arisen, one must employ various means to sever doubts and repeatedly provide enlightenment.
This requires considerable skillful rhetoric and painstaking, indirect guidance, yet even then, the practitioner remains half-inclined toward doubt.
Faith! At times one suddenly awakens, at times one is suddenly deluded; yet as one’s discernment turns deeper, the more one investigates, the more wondrous it becomes.

This continues until reaching the middle of the fourth fascicle, where this principle of skillful means (*upāya*) becomes perfectly clear and bright, and initial understanding and realization are achieved.

Thus, while the preceding scriptural passages have only served to instruct one toward such understanding and realization, they have not yet reached the point of establishing the gates of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) to instruct one in further cultivation. How could a commentator dare to act arbitrarily [in this regard]?
This specifically points to the gate of contemplation (*guanmen*) to cause one to practice it. Furthermore, the Buddha’s intention necessarily required a complete understanding (*yuanjie*).

Once correct faith had been opened and the practitioner was determined to be a suitable vessel (*dangji*), they themselves requested the gate for cultivation and progress; only then did [the Buddha] specifically point to the ear-gate as the wondrous gate for entering this principle.
He further selected and exhorted them, warning that they must not intermingle this with other various skillful means (*upāya*).
Now, why do you establish three contemplations in disorder before the ear-door has even been pointed out? Why do you confuse and disturb the minds of people?
If this is not called openly defying the Buddha’s words and erroneously transmitting the Buddha’s intent, I simply cannot believe it.
It is like a king who, about to undertake a military expedition to the east, dispatches an envoy to proclaim his imperial decree and summon all the generals to assemble.
He assembled [the officials] beneath the palace gates to await instructions regarding the divine strategy and celestial plans for deciding the victory of the eastern expedition.
The envoy rashly transmitted orders to the generals to set out immediately and proceed swiftly toward the western expedition. After some time, the King questioned the envoy:

"Why have the generals not yet arrived? The envoy replied, "On that day, the mandate was issued ordering them to proceed immediately toward the western expedition; it has been a long time since then. The King—
He was greatly incensed, deeply wondering that the envoy had mistakenly conveyed his command. This case is likewise so:

the Buddha wished to direct practitioners specifically toward the cultivation of the perfect penetration of the ear faculty (*śrotra-āyatana*), much like a king who intends to undertake an eastern expedition first reveals his wondrous strategy to awaken them to the fundamental principle, thereby establishing it as the point of entry for perfect penetration—just as a king first desires to proclaim his divine military calculations.

To deliberate upon the victory of an eastern expedition before the commentary has yet explained the perfect penetration (yuantong), and to immediately establish the three contemplations (sanguan) for one to practice, is like a messenger falsely transmitting orders to someone, commanding them to go quickly on a western expedition.

Judging from this, it is certain that this constitutes an error and a false transmission. Generally speaking, once one has commented upon the Buddhist sutras, one ought to strictly honor [the original intent].
The Buddha said: "The Buddha has never explicitly established a system of contemplation gates for people to practice.

For what reason do you falsely provide such instructions? Do you not further harbor doubts? The guest replied: "When various masters analyze and distinguish the three contemplations, they also rely solely upon their own insights.

Where this [practice] can be considered the contemplation of emptiness, they judge it to be the contemplation of emptiness, and so forth. This is like a king requesting the wisdom of Śāṇḍilya, and his minister understanding it."

If one understands and upholds this without error, why must it wait for the Tathāgata to explicitly state *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* before it can be considered contemplation (*vipaśyanā*)? Answer: It is indeed so.
Although the Buddha did not explicitly establish this, its true intent was contained within his teachings. The wise masters, acting as his ministers, were able to comprehend it.
Now, let us not dispute whether this intent is correct or not; rather, we shall simply ask: in which of these three contemplations should this be placed?
At what time is this cultivation performed? Is it cultivated prior to the Perfect Penetration (*yuan-tong*), precisely during the Perfect Penetration, or further after the Perfect Penetration?

If it were cultivated prior to the Perfect Penetration, then the preceding text would constitute the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); why then is it judged to be the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*)?
Furthermore, the Three Contemplations (*sanzhuan*) should be the skillful means for the beginner's mind, while the Perfect Penetration should be for the profound mind; why then [is it otherwise]?

This "penetration" is also called the "expedient means of the initial mind. If one is practicing within the context of perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*), then the nature of hearing fundamentally takes its essence as non-discriminative.

One simply turns the hearing back upon itself, entering directly with a single stroke; therefore, one first abandons the six consciousnesses and does not employ vitarka, vicāra, or discursive thought.
As the verse says: "Vitarka and vicāra transcend discursive thought; body and mind cannot reach them. If one were now to add...

As for the "three contemplations," they rely upon the conventional mental processes of vitarka (initial application) and vicāra (sustained application); how then could they possibly transcend the six consciousnesses?

Thus, it would be incorrect for the Tathāgata to first seek to destroy the six consciousnesses. If these were practiced after [attaining] perfect penetration, then their error would be as previously explained in the analysis of the shallow and deep stages.
Since these three periods are all devoid of utility, how can you falsely attribute such an intention to the Buddha?

Is there within this [text] that which corresponds to the Three Contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) of Tiantai? Furthermore, since that wise minister truly understood the King’s intention without error or deviation, the King would have had no need to issue further revised edicts;
he should simply have pointed to the three contemplations mentioned in the preceding text when requesting their cultivation in the subsequent passage.
Why, then, must he separately explain "hearing in reverse" (*pratikūla-śravaṇa*) as the method of cultivation? Since he has now explained it separately, [it must be distinct].

Yet, since the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) are not employed, this sufficiently proves that what was previously revealed was only the principle of the intrinsically complete essence (*prakṛti-sampad-ātmaka-tattva*), and did not encompass the three contemplations.
How could the various masters truly be the wise ministers of a universal monarch? The guest said:

"Is it a secret contemplation? [The Master] replied: "I do not deny that this is ultimately neither *śamatha* nor *vipaśyanā*.
Since Ānanda originally asked about *samādhi* and the Tathāgata originally answered regarding *samādhi*, how could *śamatha-vipaśyanā* and *samādhi-prajñā* contradict the sūtras?
However, although the terminology used here for 'samādhi' and 'contemplation' appears similar to common usage, their meaning is in fact entirely distinct. (Tiantai San)

Observing that [your position] is not of the same category as the reality [of the text], I shall now repeatedly clarify only that it is not the *Tiantai Zhiguan* (Tiantai’s Calming and Contemplation).
This does not mean that I am universally rejecting its fundamental samādhi and fundamental contemplation.

This is because if one attempts to interpret the subtle and secret observation of *śamatha* by applying the conceptual framework of Tiantai contemplation, it will create a profound barrier to the original intent of the Sūtra. Please allow me to explain this further.
I shall clarify this. First, regarding the use of the "cultivation" (xiu) aspect to explain the nature (xing): this covers approximately the first three and a half fascicles of the sutra.
The Buddha fundamentally expounded the samādhi of nature (xingding), yet various commentaries have consistently interpreted it through the lens of Tiantai’s perspective on cultivation.

If this is so, how can one expect people to suddenly grasp the samādhi of nature and recognize the treasures of their own original home? The guest replied: "Tiantai’s Three Contemplations (sanguan) specifically clarify that [all phenomena] are inherently complete within the nature."

The Perfect Teaching (Yuanli) utterly rejects the provisional vehicles and their partial, gradual approaches. How can it be said that it belongs to the provisional school and falls entirely into the category of "attainment through cultivation"?

Rather, within the context of *Tathāgata-dhyāna*, this master’s teachings are shown to be superior to those of other schools.

The gate of contemplation (*guanmen*) is also profound and subtle in its meaning, and it accords well with the school of Nature (*xingzong*). However, when compared with the present sutra, their essential purports are quite distinct.
This is because, in the Tiantai school, the three truths (*sandì*), the three contemplations (*sanguan*), and the three cessations (*sanzhǐ*) are established as mutually corresponding entities.

As for the fundamental, inherent principle-body (*lǐtǐ*), it is entirely contained within the realm of the three truths; whereas the three cessations and three contemplations are merely the meditative concentrations (*dìng*) cultivated based upon that nature.

It is not that the nature itself is said to be fixed. Now, the text of the first three and a half fascicles of this sutra elucidates the inherently complete, harmonious, and immovable essence of self-nature; this is precisely the samādhi of śamatha.

Furthermore, that which realizes and perceives this is the subtle and profound contemplation (vipaśyanā). Within this, there are indeed instances of verbal understanding and verbal realization, yet as for cultivation—

I have never previously encountered this. Now, the commentators are superficial; they fail to conduct further research and instead judge it solely by the intent of practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

How, then, can students know that this refers to the nature of meditative concentration (*dharmatā-samādhi*)? The guest said: "Having received this instruction, I shall study and savor the scriptural text.

If one speaks of them as the Three Truths, this is still relatively close to the mark, though not entirely so; for the realm of truth is fundamentally established based on the principle of inherent nature (xingju).

Just as when a person paints a portrait of their parents, it must necessarily resemble them; so too, the three stages of cessation and the three contemplations (*trividha-śamatha-vipaśyanā*) are the fruits of cultivation arising based on the principles of the Truths (*satya*).
These are like performing sacrifices, paying respect, and contemplating before a painted image.
However, the three *tathāgatagarbhas* shown in this sutra are like the actual living parents themselves; they are not even mere painted images.
"It may be that they are entirely identical when it comes to the act of worship and the thought of reverence; what interference is there [in this]? The guest said:
"The Three Truths certainly expound the principle of inherent nature (xingju). The Three Tathāgatagarbhas also expound the principle of inherent nature.
How can it be that the Three Truths are merely like a painted image, while the Three Tathāgatagarbhas are like the actual person? The Master replied: "If you do not understand this meaning..."

Then one would surely fail the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* greatly. Now, the three truths are merely the Great Master’s provisional constructs for practitioners, positing the true, the conventional, and the middle to represent the subtle, wondrous, and perfectly integrated nature of one's own mind. To realize this, one must employ the three contemplations and the three cessations;
through sustained visualization, reflection, and cultivation, only after a long time will one reach the inconceivable realm. This is its initial gateway; if one departs from it...
The six consciousnesses involve discursive thought and deliberation, such that the mind cannot find a place to rest therein. Now, the three *tathāgatagarbhas* are entirely different from this;
for their ultimate, true essence is precisely the non-discriminative nature within the six sense organs of sentient beings as they currently perceive forms and hear sounds.
When the Buddha first revealed the teaching, he first demolished the six consciousnesses, so that one does not employ any conceptual thought.
First, there is the mind of contemplative visualization; next, one proceeds directly within the faculty of the present eye-sense.

By pointing a finger upward or extending a fist, and by pointing directly at the face, one reveals the nature of seeing—which is luminous, serene, and free from discrimination—as the mind. Furthermore, by bending the fingers and waving the light, one demonstrates that this [nature] is fundamentally unmoving and so forth.
All of these methods are intended to cause the practitioner to personally see their own mind face-to-face. Thus, Ānanda first attained awakening.
My own account is like that of a child who has lost its mother and then beholds her again; how is this not the same as seeing one's parents in person before one's eyes?

Why, then, labor over painted images and mental visualizations? If one abandons one's parents in their actual presence and fails to pay them reverence, yet instead bows to a painted image, this is a great perversion.
This would be to take the three Tathāgata-garbhas as the Three Truths, which is still not [correct].
"It is acceptable. How much more so when it is confused with the three types of cessation-and-contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*)? The guest said:

'The Three Tathāgatagarbhas represent a progressive entry into the ultimate principle of profound, subtle, and perfect interfusion. How can you say that the very nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*) shown at the outset is its substance?
I smiled and said: 'Is this not where the root of your delusion lies? It is precisely because the various masters highly extol what comes later [that they overlook the beginning]...'"
One conceals the mind, failing to realize that the very nature of the faculties previously shown—such as the faculty of sight—is non-dual in its essence.

One simply asserts that there exists something separate from the nature of the faculties; thus, during practice, one does not further employ the nature of the faculties, but instead intends to conceal that nature.

By establishing the Three Truths and initiating the Three Contemplations, one considers this to be perfectly subtle and wondrous, yet remains unaware that one is once again falling into the conceptualization and observation of the conscious mind (*vijñāna-citta*).
In contemplating this realm, you have exhausted the essential intent of the sutras and utterly lost the Buddha’s heart. Now, I pray that you will clarify this through an analogy.
Suppose there were a golden lion coated in mud; its golden form would be completely hidden.

Suddenly, a wise person, wishing to reveal the golden body to others, takes a cloth and polishes its eyes until the golden color shines through. Then, there would be no one who does not rejoice and leap for joy. Furthermore...
One rubs it; by doing so, it gradually opens wide, its entire body radiating a blazing light.

Yet, in the end, it is no different in color from the gold used for the eye-patch at the beginning, nor is it different in substance. By using this analogy to examine the intent of the sutra, the meaning becomes brilliantly clear:
one thereby knows that although the three *tathāgatagarbhas* are fully revealed as perfectly interfused, their entire body and great function remain as they were.
In the initial manifestation of the nature of seeing within the faculties, there are established two aspects. This is specifically because words cannot reveal [the truth] all at once;

rather, they are unfolded sequentially, from the subtle to the manifest, much like polishing gold. Furthermore, one should know that the natures of seeing, hearing, and so forth are merely partial designations for the *ālaya-vijñāna* (the storehouse mind), yet in reality, they possess no partial substance.
This is just as the Patriarchs directly pointed to the human mind, saying it is "right here."

That which is in the eye is called seeing; that which is in the ear is called hearing. This principle is indeed certain. Therefore, when the Buddha answered the request for cultivation, he taught that one should turn back the inverted faculty of hearing;
this very nature of the hearing-faculty is the nature of the three Tathāgata-garbhas. How could there be any distinct entities?
The guest said: "If this is so, then even the Three Truths are not yet the Three Contemplations; what connection could there be?
Why did the Indian monk previously transmit this sutra as being identical to the Three Contemplations of Tiantai? I answer: There are two ways to infer the meaning of this.
First, the intellectual clarity and obscurity of people in India and China are often similar; how can we know that the Indian monk was not himself deluded by what appeared to be correct?
It is not so. Second, if he merely meant that it is roughly equivalent to the Three Truths of Tiantai, then his statement is not erroneous.
Why must one insist that it is identical to the Three Contemplations? It is simply that later generations have taken up empty echoes and mistakenly fashioned them into the Three Contemplations;
this is not the fault of the Indian monk. The guest said: "Ānanda asked about the wondrous samādhi for attaining Buddhahood, and the Buddha replied..."

If it were necessarily a perfect and fixed [teaching], then *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna* would require that mentioning one immediately implies the three, and speaking of the three immediately implies the one;
only then could it be considered "perfect. Why, then, are the three names now each opened up separately? How can this be called a perfect and fixed teaching?

Answer: Your previous views were submerged in delusion; your fundamental basis is not shallow. What is there to wonder at in your profound confusion? It is truly because the natures and practices of former people were...
Since he was unable to distinguish between them, he insisted that they were definitively identical to the Three Contemplations (*san guan*) of Tiantai.
Furthermore, seeing that this samādhi also has three names, he failed to investigate or scrutinize the texts and meanings to determine whether they were the same or not;

instead, upon seeing a single name, he would arbitrarily supplement it to make three, forcefully asserting that "raising one is [raising] three" and "speaking of three is [speaking of] one," merely wishing to force a conformity with the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) of the Tiantai school.

It is merely a marvelous image. Judging from this, not only do they fail to understand the fundamental purport of why this samādhi constitutes the Perfect (yuan), but even the Tiantai school itself has likely not yet fully mastered it.
This is because the three contemplations (*sanguan*) of the Tiantai school must be like the celestial eye of Maheśvara—neither vertical nor horizontal—only then can they be considered "Perfect.
This is because all three are instantaneously complete and devoid of temporal sequence.

It is not vertical, for all three mutually encompass one another and are not listed in parallel; thus, it is not horizontal. Now, to treat each point as merely equal without clarifying their comprehensive integration is to fall entirely into the horizontal view.
This indicates that even the Tiantai school has not yet reached a thorough understanding; how then can one expect them to clarify the essential meaning of this sutra?

Furthermore, within the Tiantai school’s Three Contemplations (*sanguan*), it is taught that "raising one is [to realize] all three" and "speaking of three is [to realize] the one"—this was indeed the Master’s own [teaching].
He spoke this himself; it was not based on the annotations of others. Now, according to the Tathāgata’s own words, he never stated that the three names—śamatha and so forth—possess such meanings.

These [interpretations] are all the result of later generations failing to understand the perfect intent of this samādhi, which is entirely independent of the three names being mutually inclusive, and thus they falsely imitated the Tiantai system to establish this view. The guest said: "As for this samādhi..."
With what intention is this considered the ultimate perfection? The answer is: the three *tathāgatagarbhas* are clearly and manifestly revealed;

first they are disclosed through a gradual sequence, and subsequently they are shown collectively as perfectly manifest. All of these are inherently complete by nature, and do not arise from cultivation.
If one explains it according to this principle, raising one is immediately three, and speaking of three is immediately one; they are neither vertical nor horizontal, which is most appropriate.
Furthermore, regarding the ultimate meaning of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*), there has never been anything that surpasses this.

How can one abandon this meaning and erroneously claim that the "perfect" (*yuan*) consists merely in the simultaneous presence of three names? The guest asked: "According to the Buddha's own mind, on what basis is this established?"
Question: Regarding these three names, the answer is that based on a rough examination of the points of inquiry, the three names appear to be no different.

However, when one seeks the answers within the various scriptures, the three meanings naturally reveal themselves as being distinctly different. One should know that the Tathāgata established these three names in reference to the three periods—beginning, middle, and end—of attaining the Great Samādhi.
That is to say, in reference to the initial opening of the understanding of the inherently endowed nature-samādhi, it is termed "Śamatha" (Calm).
*Śamatha* refers to entering this nature-concentration (*dharmatā-samādhi*) by way of the middle [stage]; *samādhi* refers to it by way of the subsequent maintenance;
and *dhyāna* refers to the cultivation and realization of this nature-concentration. The guest asked:

"If the perfect principle of concentration resides solely within the three *tathāgatagarbhas*, and since only these three are present within *śamatha* in this scripture, then should *śamatha* alone be considered to possess the perfect meaning, while the latter two..."
[The opponent] says: "In the *Śamatha* [section], there is no mention of the Three Treasuries (*tripiṭaka*). Therefore, the subsequent [explanation] should not be complete. [I] answer:
The fact that the interpretations of various schools do not accord with one another from beginning to end is precisely the same as your own confusion.

You assume that what is discussed later is entirely different from what was shown earlier, failing to realize that within the *śamatha* section, this teaching reveals that there are originally three *tathāgatagarbhas*. Within the *samādhi* section, it is the teaching...
Entering this, there are originally three Tathāgata-garbhas. Within *dhyāna*, these teachings maintain the practice and realization of these original three Tathāgata-garbhas;
from beginning to end, they are pervasively one single Garbha-nature. How could it be that what existed before is non-existent afterward?

If what is entered and realized later were not the Garbha-nature of what preceded it, then why would there have been the need to extensively expound upon the Garbha-nature prior to entry and realization? And...

After attaining awakening, what is the nature of that which is entered and realized? Generally speaking, the ancient commentators on the latter sections of the sutras frequently disregard the preceding parts.
For instance, when discussing the Three Piṭakas, they have already failed to understand that these correspond to the fundamental natures previously indicated at the outset;
nor have they ever clarified that one merely enters the nature of the Piṭakas or has set forth the various stages. Furthermore, [they fail to see]...
How could one know that this document [the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*] takes Perfect Enlightenment as its basis to cultivate and realize the nature of the treasury? Consider this:
since Ānanda had already used the metaphor of a magnificent mansion for the aforementioned nature of the treasury, it follows that "perfect penetration" (Skt.

*pratyavekṣaṇā*) serves to enter the door of that mansion, while the fifty-five stages serve to ascend into the hall of the mansion and enter its inner chambers. How could it be otherwise than departing from that preceding mansion?

There is indeed a destination. Since the nature of the single treasury (ekakṣaya-dhātu) is identical from beginning to end, then from beginning to end it is simply the one perfectly interfused and determinate nature.
Why, then, would it be perfect in the beginning but not perfect in the end? The refutation of the lack of correspondence is hereby concluded.
Second, there are various forms of indeterminate delusion; this further has two parts. First is the refutation of the lack of determination regarding consciousness. Now, as for "the one..."
In the Great Vehicle teachings, the distinction between the provisional and the ultimate depends entirely upon whether one recognizes [the true nature] or fails to recognize it.

This is precisely because sentient beings turn their backs on Nirvana and sink forever into the cycle of birth and death; this is entirely due to both body and mind being fundamentally mistaken. Thus, the *Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* states:
"One falsely identifies the five aggregates and the four great elements as the characteristic of the body, and the discrimination of sensory objects as the characteristic of the mind. This is so.
Although both are errors, while the error regarding the body is easily understood by people, the error regarding the mind is difficult for them to know.

Thus, that the six consciousnesses are not the mind is something not only unrecognized by those within the realms of humans and devas, but even the two vehicles of the supramundane have not yet fully realized it.
As for the bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings, although they know there is a distinct ālayavijñāna, as for...
To take this as the substance of contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā*) likewise cannot transcend these six consciousnesses.

That is to say, if one takes a mind of arising and ceasing as the fundamental cause for cultivation, one will ultimately be unable to attain the fruit of permanence. For this reason, the ultimate fruits of the provisional teachings merely coincide with the two practices of the Perfect [Teaching].
Thus, how could the wondrous purport of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* alone be difficult to believe and difficult to understand in its profound depths? It is already so even in this...
Regarding the first section, "Refuting Consciousness": this involves successive hesitation, which prevents the formation of decisive faith;

it involves successive confusion and entanglement, which prevents the attainment of clear understanding. The guest said: "Among those who study the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, who does not know its initial refutation of consciousness?
Why then do you speak of characteristics that are difficult to believe and difficult to understand? I replied: "If your deep faith were bright and lucid, why would you not perceive it?"

Regarding the errors of the old commentary, [the author] says: "Please show me. [The author] replies: "For example, when the Buddha asked Ānanda, 'What was the initial condition for you to resolve upon awakening?

and Ānanda answered that he resolved upon awakening by taking the Buddha’s physical marks and signs as his condition—this was because the Buddha merely wished to take up the consciousness that conditions those marks to refute it as being the mind itself.
It was not a rebuke for improperly clinging to the marks and signs as having real existence. The old... [text ends].

The commentary abruptly interrupts [the argument] by stating: "If the marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and appearances (*nimitta*) truly exist and their arising and ceasing are manifest, then by relying on these one generates the aspiration for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*) and securely proceeds toward the fruit of permanence.
If this were the Buddha’s original intention, then the Buddha would have immediately refuted the thirty-two marks as being not the Tathāgata;

furthermore, he would have cautioned that one must not grasp them as truly existent and must not rely upon them to generate the aspiration for enlightenment. Only such a commentary would be [correct].
This is not incorrect. Now that you have understood this, you are entirely without such an intention; would this not be a great error?

Furthermore, you cite a later passage—where it says that taking a mind of arising and ceasing as a cause fails to obtain the fruit of permanence—to prove your point. You do not realize that this passage specifically refutes the errors of employing the *vijñānas* (consciousnesses);

it is by no means a reprimand for the fault of clinging to appearances (*nimitta*). Thus, you are confused throughout both the preceding and following sections, treating everything as a refutation of consciousness.
The essential meaning was thus transformed into the school of "shattering appearances" (poxiang). Is this not a state of confused delusion?

How could it ever have clarified the correct intent that shatters consciousness (*vijñāna*) rather than mind (*citta*)? Although the *Huìjiě* places this commentary at the beginning and likewise says nothing of its error, it later adds:
Ānanda’s perception of these signs was a vision that discriminates based on sensory objects. The mind he gave rise to was precisely a mind of deluded thought and grasping after conditions.

This is what is repeatedly pursued and refuted in the subsequent sections concerning the "seven investigations" and "eight arguments. Now that the refutation of the mind is understood, [the text proceeds].

This would then not be the refutation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Why, moreover, do you simultaneously adopt the commentary on the refutation of characteristics? Although this seems like understanding, it is nonetheless not definitive;
thus, there remains an irresolvable bifurcation. Is this not a state of hesitation that has failed to produce true faith?

Furthermore, one must not mistakenly conflate the eyes previously discussed with the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*), thereby claiming that the "eight returns" analysis of seeing is identical to the "seven inquiries" refutation.
Moreover, one should not situate the nature of seeing under the name of "discrimination based on objects," for such discrimination belongs solely to consciousness;
rather, the nature of seeing revealed by the Buddha is fundamentally pure.
The pure and the neutral [states] both lack the function of discriminating objects. As the Buddha said: "It is simply like a mirror, which performs no separate analysis.

These [explanations] represent the ultimate confusion arising from a failure to clarify the characteristics of dharmas (dharmalakṣaṇa); the error is not slight. There is no leisure to explain them all at once;

for now, I shall clarify the reason why [the mind] does not know, thereby refuting [the notion of] consciousness. Furthermore, the old commentary states: "Ānanda was weary of his extensive learning..."
Yet they rejoice in wondrous concentration. When the Tathāgata wishes to expound this meaning, he first interrogates them regarding false conditions;
thus, he asks about the cause of the arising of the mind and the perception of signs. This serves as the fundamental basis for ceasing distraction and entering stillness.

If one observes the initial interrogation concerning false conditions and concludes that it is merely the refutation of consciousness, yet notes that the final statement speaks of "the fundamental basis for ceasing distraction and entering stillness," then one’s understanding is still not precise. This is truly because the Tathāgata...
Breaking through consciousness does not merely mean halting the mind’s scattering toward objects to enter a state of tranquil concentration. It is said:

"Even if one were to extinguish all seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, and inwardly maintain a state of profound stillness, this would still be a mere shadow of conceptualization regarding mental objects (*dharmas*). Furthermore, it says:

Although those who practice may currently achieve the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), they fail to exhaust their outflows and become Arhats because they all cling to these deluded thoughts, mistaking them for reality.
Is it not the case that one merely considers the cessation of distraction and entry into stillness to be sufficient?
You should know that the Buddha’s intent was to clarify that this consciousness—whether in a state of distraction or meditative stillness—is entirely not the true mind. However...

These are but dust-like reflections; they possess no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). If one wishes to cultivate *śamatha* and the other [meditative practices], one must first completely relinquish this mind and not employ it.
However, there is a profound reason why the Buddha necessarily takes the consciousness that has resolved to leave the household life (*pravrajyā-citta*) and shatters it;
this has not been clarified since antiquity. It is truly because this consciousness possesses the greatest capacity for both supreme goodness and inferior evil, and thus it must be shattered.
If that which is inferior and evil necessarily retains that which is superior and wholesome, how could the superior and wholesome ever exist apart from the inferior and evil?

Furthermore, the functions of this consciousness regarding the superior and wholesome are briefly of five kinds: first, the mind that takes the physical marks of the Buddha as its object; second, the mind that takes the Buddha’s vocal teachings as its object;
third, the mind that hears the Dharma and attains realization; fourth, the mind that ceases distraction and enters stillness; and fifth, [the mind] beyond the realms...
Regarding the mind that seeks realization—these various superior and wholesome cognitive minds—the Buddha has refuted them all in this sutra.

Therefore, the initial refutation of the mind generated by those who have left the household life specifically refutes the first [type of] mind: that which takes the physical marks of the Buddha as its object.
As the text below states: "As you now listen to my Dharma, this is a discrimination arising from sound. This refutes the second...
