Second, it refers to the mind that takes the Buddha’s vocal teachings as its object. Furthermore, the later passage states: "Ānanda does not abandon his realization of the Buddha manifesting the sound of the Dharma.

The Buddha tells him that this Dharma also takes [the sense organs] as its objects, even up to taking sound as its object; apart from sound, there is no intrinsic nature. This immediately refutes the third point:
the mind that realizes and understands the Dharma upon hearing it. Moreover, the later passage says: "Even if one were to extinguish all seeing and hearing, [it would still be considered...]"
"Distinguishing the affairs of reflections" refers to the refutation of the fourth [type of mind]: the mind that abandons distraction and enters stillness. Furthermore, the subsequent passage states:
"Though one may manifest the nine successive attainments (navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti), this is all due to grasping at this as being true reality.

This refutes the fifth [type of mind]: the mind that seeks realization outside the realms. If even these five are all to be refuted and eliminated, how could other inferior and evil [minds] possibly exist?
There may be some remaining doubt. However, it is essential to understand that the Buddha’s intent in refuting [these views] was not to do so because these five functions possess any fault or error.
Indeed, these five functions remain supreme and virtuous merits; what fault or error could they have?
It is only when people mistake this consciousness of active functioning for the true, fundamental mind that a great error occurs, leading to boundless birth and death.
All of this is due to a mistaken identification, for they take this consciousness to be the mind. As the Buddha rebuked him, saying: "Alas, Ānanda! This is not your mind;
it is merely the false conceptualization of the characteristics of external objects. Even to the point of identifying a thief as one's own son, one thus undergoes the cycle of rebirth.
This is precisely the Tathāgata’s fundamental intent in refuting [the notion of a self-mind]. However, there are two reasons why he necessarily refutes it by means of the five functions.
[The Master] said: "First, if one were to negate its function, then consciousness would have no characteristic; from what, then, could one apply the negation?

Second, these five functions are the superior and wholesome capacities of this consciousness. Fearing that people might value these capacities and consequently become attached to and begrudge this consciousness, unable to relinquish it entirely, [the teaching] merely applies the negation from these five functions.
If one does not begrudge them, then deluded consciousness will be relinquished completely without remainder. For this reason..."
Because the meaning is profoundly deep and difficult to discern, the ancient commentators failed to understand it.

Seeing that [the text] speaks of "arousing the mind from seeing marks," they refuted it by searching for faults at the very point where the mind is said to be aroused, claiming that "seeing marks truly exists" and so forth.

How could they know that the intent of the refutation does not lie in the attachment to marks as being existent, but rather lies solely in the attachment to consciousness as being the mind? This, then, is the Buddha’s definitive teaching.

The Illumination [Samādhi] completely shatters and eliminates this mind, without the slightest intention of indulgence or lingering delay. Yet, alas, sentient beings have clung to it as their own mind since beginningless kalpas;
beyond this, they know not that there exists a separate true mind, and thus find it extremely difficult to relinquish.
Although the Tathāgata exerts his utmost power to break and seize it away, they are still unable to give rise to decisive faith or achieve decisiveness.
There are many who, having abandoned [their practice], continue to waver in doubt, clinging with stinginess and hesitation; such cases are common enough and not worth remarking upon.

As for the commentator on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, who possessed the talent for composition and had accumulated years of training in both meditation and exegesis, he devoted more than twenty or thirty years to his endeavor to synthesize and explain the teachings.
Yet, when he reached this point and saw the Buddha shatter this very mind, he was so excessively startled that he instead attempted to rescue it.

Regarding this, it is said: To examine its origin, delusion has no self-nature; its entire substance is the Truth itself. Thus, there is nothing to be destroyed when one speaks of "destroying," and ignorance is itself illumination.

Even as the World-Honored One previously stated that sentient beings do not know the true mind and instead employ various delusive thoughts, he now says they cling to these delusive thoughts, mistakenly taking them for reality.
If this is so, does it follow that delusive thoughts are truly not the true mind? One should know that regarding all phenomena...

There is neither gain nor loss; delusion and awakening depend upon the person. If one possesses sharp faculties and thin afflictions, they will realize that the very substance of delusive thought is, directly beneath it, the true mind.
Although these words may have some logical basis, they should not be uttered at this point;
to place them here would utterly destroy the essential intent of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, for at this juncture, sentient beings are precisely in the state of clinging and stinginess.
At this moment, when doubts are still wavering and stability has not yet been attained, how can one bear to hear words that add frost to snow?
Such talk causes many to fall into hesitation and leads many to further delusion. Indeed, from the very beginning of the sutra, the Tathāgata has expended immense effort;
seven times he demolished their notion of a fixed location, directly rebuked them for having no mind, and exerted every power to demonstrate that they have no essence.

Now, Gongkeng has revealed its entire essence and further stated that it is precisely the true mind (*tathatā-citta*). Does this not cause people to once again form the fixed view that it is indeed the true mind?
Moreover, although Ānanda had previously engaged in strenuous debate and raised doubts, it was only upon reaching this point that he attained a state of silent self-realization;
there is a message here of letting go and casting everything aside. For the clever practitioners of the末法 (mofa, final age)...
Śeng heard this passage in the sutra and likewise shared this view. Upon hearing these words, how could he not stubbornly hold on and refuse to let go?
He believed that even the Tathāgata’s refutations were merely provisional meanings, and that this consciousness was originally the true mind.

Whenever he encountered statements in the sutras that seemed to refute it, he would immediately use those very words as a defense. Not only did this fail to bring about a definitive resolution, but...
This would certainly result in abandoning [the teaching] and returning once more to definitive attachment. Would this not utterly destroy the fundamental intent of the Tathāgata?

The guest said: "If the mind of consciousness is entirely illusory, it must ultimately be shattered. Yet, after the subsequent sections on the Four Elements and the Seven Elements, why do you further allow that they are all identical to the Tathāgatagarbha-mind?
Tianru replied: "The root of your doubt lies precisely here. This is truly because..."

Thus, the two gates of skillful means (*upāya*) and equality (*samatā*) have not yet been fully realized. "Skillful means" refers to the intention of definitive discernment; "equality" refers to the intention of universal integration.
At the beginning of the sutra, consciousness is refuted as being entirely delusory and its use is prohibited; this is the intention of definitive discernment within the gate of skillful means.

At the end of the sutra, it is permitted that consciousness is also true, and both are equally termed the "storehouse nature" (*ālaya-dhātu*); this is the intention of universal integration within the gate of equality.
Furthermore, if one follows the Buddha’s intent without losing its proper sequence, then the two gates may mutually support one another;

if one contravenes the Buddha’s intent through artificiality, perversity, and disorder, then the two gates will instead be mutually opposed. The guest asked: "What is meant by 'mutually supporting' when following the intent? The answer is:
Although consciousness resides within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), it serves as the root of birth and death. If it is not eliminated, one will practice erroneously and in confusion.

Because "steaming sand to make rice" is the reason for its eradication, it serves as the expedient means (*upāya*) for entering the Perfect [Teaching]. Furthermore, although consciousness is fundamentally illusory, how could it exist apart from what is manifested by the Mind-only?
If one does not integrate [consciousness] into [the Mind], then there would be phenomena outside the Mind;

since the nature of the Sage is not permeated by such [duality], integration ensures that the expedient means do not become mired in stagnation. Thus, from beginning to end, all is merely in accord with the Buddha’s words, each forming a subtle perfection.
"Is it not the case that these [two] mutually support one another? The guest asked: 'What do you mean by saying that to contravene the intent is to act in mutual opposition? I replied:
'Suppose, for instance, that at the very moment of definitive discernment, one were to oppose [the teaching] by adopting a later, superficial meaning, saying:

"Since both are the *ālaya-vijñāna* (storehouse consciousness), how could this truly be false? Why must it be refuted? In doing so, the falsehood would become fundamentally entrenched and the cultivation of the truth would be forever blocked. Based on this.
This refers to the time when the Tathāgata later merges [with the dharmadhātu]. One may also take the meaning of the previous *upāya* (expedient means) to counter this, saying:

"The root of birth and death—how could it truly be the *tathāgatagarbha*-mind? Why must it be universally gathered? If one says this, then the *upāya* becomes mired in confusion and the perfect purport (*pariniṣpanna-artha*) is forever separated.
This would then repudiate the sublime purports before and after the Buddha’s teaching, resulting entirely in a contradiction of one's own words. Is this not so?

They are mutually contradictory; one should know this. The universal integration that encompasses all phenomena must be exhaustive, while the skillful means of discerning what to adopt and what to reject must be rigorous.
The subsequent universal inclusion does not obstruct the prior refutation; how could one doubt the former on account of the latter?
Is it not the case that you definitively rely on the Buddha’s refutation?

If you insist that the later [text] refers to the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) while doubting that the former does not definitively refute it, then the two great elements of water and fire would likewise be the *ālayavijñāna*.

Consequently, those who revere water and serve fire would not be definitive non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). How could one who practices the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* even permit the reverence of water and service of fire? Thus, regarding water...
Although fire is latent within the heart, if one reveres and serves it, one will certainly fall into false views and fail to achieve perfect enlightenment;

thus, it must certainly be refuted and rejected. It is just as the six consciousnesses, though they contain the mind, if one employs and cultivates them, one will certainly be stalled in birth and death and fail to achieve Bodhi;
these too must certainly be refuted and rejected. Why, O Guest, are you so deluded?

Question: Although consciousness is stored within the mind, it is ultimately not employed in cultivation. Later, when Śāriputra and others appear, why do they again rely upon it to achieve the six kinds of perfect penetration?

Answer: This is also one point where various schools harbor lingering doubts. Since Mañjuśrī has already selected and eliminated [the unsuitable methods], why trouble yourself with further questioning?
If you do not understand this, you may investigate the subsequent verses and the commentaries on those passages.

Thus, there is nothing that is not clarified. Second, the manifestation of seeing is indeterminate. This is because after the refutation of consciousness, the Buddha fundamentally intended to reveal that seeing is the mind;
yet the old commentaries all state that the preceding passage already refuted the deluded mind, and what follows now refutes the deluded seeing.
To use what is manifest to refute [the misconception] is no small delusion; therefore, it must be clarified.
Now, since the Tathāgata has already refuted the consciousness that Ānanda had long firmly clung to as being the mind, declaring it to be not the mind, Ānanda then asked the Tathāgata:
"What, then, is this tranquil, eternal, wondrously luminous mind? At this point, the Tathāgata necessarily had to provide him with something that is indeed the mind.
As soon as the matter is settled—if it were not so, one would simply continue to demand [an answer] without ceasing—why then do you again raise objections?
Furthermore, he has set aside his former attachments all at once and is single-mindedly demanding: "Which of these is the mind? So, what is there to refute in that?
If one claims that this moment must be refuted, then one has not even understood the sequence of the question and answer;

how could such a person possibly manifest the Buddha’s intent? Furthermore, the Buddha originally pointed out a segment of the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*) within the faculty of the eye for others.

This demonstrates that whether possessing eyes or being without eyes, whether in light or in darkness, its essence remains eternally present. It is the solitary radiance of spiritual brilliance, utterly transcending the sense organs and their objects.
This differs from the preceding view, which held that once the mind is detached from objects, it lacks its own substantiality. Finally, he restates this correct principle.

He then made this determination: "This is the mind, not the eye. Because sentient beings in their daily lives know only that this faculty of seeing is the eye and do not know it is the mind—what is called "being deluded by taking oneself for an object"—the Tathāgata pointed it out afresh and said to them:
"When you ask what is the mind, this very nature of seeing is your mind. Why do you consistently regard it only as the eye?"
[The Master] said: "I understand. You do not understand this mind. From now on, you should know that this seeing is the mind;
it is not the eye. Previously, I refuted that consciousness is not the mind; now, I reveal that this seeing is the mind. One is negation and one is affirmation;

they are diametrically opposed. One is refuted and one is revealed; their meanings are starkly different. This is extremely clear and fluent, and it is also consistent with the logic of question and answer."
However, regarding the force of these words: why have all the masters for over a thousand years unanimously declared that this section is for the purpose of shattering false views?

Generally, wherever there is a refutation, there must be an object of attachment. For instance, as previously mentioned, because the mind-consciousness arises dependent on causes, its objects are clearly known and its attachments are firm;
therefore, various refutations are employed to strip away that stubborn adherence. Now, as for this nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*), Ānanda has demonstrated it to be identical with sound.

I have heard that, in ordinary times, you were unaware that this faculty of seeing is the mind. Who, then, could give rise to attachment? And what is there for you to refute in another? This is utterly meaningless.

Here, within the discussion of the sense-faculties (*indriya*), the essence of seeing is pointed out. The text contains ten major sections in total, which most clearly demonstrate that the nature of seeing is unmoving, indestructible, and non-returning.
The Tathāgata’s true compassion seeks only to reach those who are ready to receive it.
This means that one abandons the previously clung-to deluded consciousness and takes up this newly manifested nature of seeing, holding fast to it and regarding it as the true original mind.
This is because there is a fear that [the practitioner] might be unwilling to hold fast to it; how could there be any intention to refute it? Please examine the following text.
Ānanda still remained hesitant and unwilling to accept this, repeatedly asking: "How can I know that this is my true nature? Then he asked:
"If what I see must be my true self, then what are this present body and mind of mine? And again he asked:
"What difference is there between this and the 'dark principle' (*tattva*) or the 'true self' (*ātman*) of the Brahmins of old? Such doubts and perplexities were shifting and unsettled, as if—

In this section, [the Master] successively resolves doubts and repeatedly reveals the wondrous nature, leaving no leisure for [the interlocutor] to reproach him for failing to grasp it or to urge him to accept and recognize it;
how then could he dare to offer even a slight refutation? Thus, these ten successive rounds are all intended to reveal the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*).
Yet, all existing commentaries collectively mistake them for a refutation of seeing, claiming that the subsequent "seven investigations and eight distinctions" constitute the core.

This refers to the successive and thorough refutation [of delusions]. Furthermore, to provide a detailed analysis of why the false mind is refuted first and the false views are refuted later, three points are presented.
The first point is as follows: the mind is the source of delusion and is the fundamental basis of the attachment to a self (*pudgala-grāha*); therefore, it must be refuted first.

However, one does not realize that the basis of the attachment to a self actually resides in the seventh consciousness (*manas-vijñāna*). Now, by refuting only the first six consciousnesses, what [connection] is there with that [seventh consciousness]?

"Good. The second point says: Mind belongs to the category of mental factors (*caitta*) and pervades all three natures; therefore, it was refuted first. Vision, however, is merely the faculty of the eye and belongs only to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*);
therefore, it was refuted later. This already seems to mistake the essence of vision revealed by the Tathāgata for a delusory, mundane material phenomenon (*rūpa-dharma*).

Consequently, it is inferior to the six consciousnesses and the mind-king (*citta-rāja*). One does not realize that [vision] is the faculty within which the Tathāgata has revealed [the nature of reality]."
The wondrous nature is precisely the *ālayavijñāna*, which is the *tathāgatagarbha* mind; how could it possibly be inferior to the six consciousnesses?

Recently, I have observed that in certain editions of books, the "eye faculty" (*cakṣurindriya*) has been erroneously changed to "eye-consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñāna*). If this were indeed the word "consciousness," the transgression would be boundless;
yet even those who are ignorant do not realize it is an error—how lamentable! Thirdly, [the text] now refutes delusion.
When he sees, he cites the example of a blind man staring into darkness to demonstrate that the nature of seeing is not extinguished;

even when he raises his hand and causes light to fly about, he shows that this nature is without movement. This intent seems to treat deluded seeing and the nature of seeing as two distinct phenomena:
it refutes the former while demonstrating the non-extinction and immovability of the latter. Upon close examination, however, the Tathāgata...
In the "Chapter on the Blind Man Gazing into Darkness," it is simply pointed out that the nature of seeing resides within the eye-faculty itself;
it clarifies that this nature is entirely unrelated to the eye-faculty or to light and darkness, being in its entirety nothing but the mind, with no second dharma existing apart from it.

To which phrase do you refer when saying it describes false vision? Or to which phrase do you refer when saying it breaks through the nature of seeing as a distinct, superior dharma that must be manifested?
Since you claim that both gazing into darkness and seeing flying lights are both manifestations of seeing, then according to the full text, all of them manifest this very meaning.
Where else, then, could you find a passage to refute seeing? Furthermore, since "immovability" is already...

If "manifesting and seeing" (*xiǎnjiàn*) refers to the eight major sections beginning with "neither extinguished nor returning," then all of these would be instances of manifesting and seeing; upon what basis, then, does the supplementary note rely [on this]?
Furthermore, does it take the passage that uses the "eight returns" to analyze seeing as being of the same category as the "seven interrogations" that sequentially refute it?

One fears that its intention might be to use "manifesting" itself as the refutation. However, refuting is like impeaching the wicked and corrupt, while manifesting is like recommending the virtuous and worthy; they are distinct in the world.

How could there ever be such a thing as a recommendation that is simultaneously a censure? Examining these three meanings together, it is evident that the characteristics of the dharmas are not clarified;
the refutation and the manifestation are muddled and confused, and the errors are manifest. How could this be difficult to see?

Such annotations as these abound throughout the text, beyond the capacity for full refutation. With such an understanding, how can one hope for him to elucidate the profundities of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*?

How profound! Thus, this scripture has long been subjected to misinterpretation; therefore, I cannot help but briefly clarify it. To examine the reasons for its resulting confusion, there are roughly four points.

First, at the beginning of the refutation of consciousness, both the mind and the eyes are interrogated together. Consequently, some claim that the Buddha’s intention was to refute both the mind and the eyes simultaneously.
Since the mind was refuted first, they argue that the eyes must now be refuted next, asserting that the eye is itself the act of seeing.
First, because the Buddha raised his fist as an analogy for seeing, [the opponent] concluded that everything from this point onward constitutes the "refutation of views.

Second, because the Buddha cited the example of a blind person looking into darkness to demonstrate that the manifestation of vision is not the eye itself—thereby appearing to refute the eye—the opponent claimed that this was undoubtedly the "refutation of views.

Third, while the Buddha intended to reveal that vision has no place of return, he first employed a method of alternation (suppression and exaltation), stating: "Although this vision is not the sublime [nature]..."

The mind of discernment: it is like the second moon, which is not the reflection of the moon. Now, although upon first hearing this they realize that their own seeing is not the wondrous mind, they still dare not recognize this seeing as the mind.
Furthermore, hearing that it is like the second moon, they then suspect that this seeing is entirely false.
They assume that apart from this seeing there exists a separate true mind, which is merely made manifest by borrowing the seeing; because of this, they consequently give rise to both mind and seeing.

This mutually clarifies the teaching that [the nature of seeing] is fundamentally within the mind. Fourth, following the tenfold clarification of seeing, the Buddha explains the confusion regarding whether "seeing" is itself "seeing.
He first states that the wandering through the world of saṃsāra arises entirely from two kinds of false seeing, and thus concludes that this seeing is, in its entirety, false.
Furthermore, he collectively judges all the preceding passages on the tenfold clarification of seeing as being about the mind.
In order to refute false views, it is stated that they are identical [to those refuted] through the sevenfold investigation (*saptabhaṅgī*) and various successive refutations.

Because of this, the various masters harbor these four delusions within their chests; consequently, they all uniformly categorize them within the section on "Seeing by Raising the Fist" (*jūken rui ken shō*), collectively designating them as refutations of false views.
Although the designation is fixed, when one reaches the detailed explanation following the text, it becomes clearly evident once again that these are all intended to reveal [the truth].
Regarding the phrase "seeing the wondrous place," [the commentator] further follows the Buddha’s explanation to manifest "seeing.

Consequently, he causes the student to observe that while the heading (*biao*) entirely negates seeing, the explanation (*shi*) instead manifests it; thus, the heading and explanation are completely inconsistent, and both the negation and the manifestation lack any definitive conclusion.
Furthermore, according to the commentary, mind and seeing appear to be two distinct dharmas; yet upon examining the text, mind and seeing are fundamentally...
It has never been resolved. These four delusions are the root of doubt that has remained unsettled for a thousand years; let us now attempt to uproot them. First:
regarding the refutation of consciousness while simultaneously interrogating both mind and eyes—this is not intended to refute both mind and eyes together.

Rather, it seeks to identify the locus of the mind upon which [the opponent] clings and to refute it there. This is done for fear that, because the mind cannot be seen, one might resort to evasion; therefore, the eyes are included.
To illustrate that which is visible and has a fixed location, let us use an analogy to resolve and clarify that the mind has a fixed location, just as the eyes are located on the face.
The Buddha posed the question: "Where are the mind and the eyes now located? Ānanda replied:
"The physical eyes, composed of the four elements, are situated only on my face; thus, the consciousness-mind truly resides within the body. From this...
Since the Tathāgata has already understood where the mind resides, he consequently refutes the notion that the mind does not reside within, and so forth.
He no longer specifically mentions the eyes; rather, this is merely an elliptical expression intended to exemplify the underlying intent of refuting [the mind's location] in its entirety.

If one were to insist that the eyes must be mentioned in succession with the mind before being refuted, then the previous statement that consciousness is within the body would immediately refute its not being within the body. The preceding...
To say that the eyes are located on the surface of the face is likewise refuted by the fact that they do not reside there;
yet, such a statement is certainly absent from the text, so how could such a principle even exist? Thus, to take this as the basis for the refutation of [the view of] seeing is undoubtedly an error.
Second, when the Buddha cited the example of a blind person looking into the darkness, he merely demonstrated that although the eye is absent, seeing does not cease.
It has never been that seeing is not the eye; since it is not the eye, it is precisely the mind.

Therefore, when responding to the seeker’s request for the wondrously luminous mind, the intent was not to refute the eye as the primary meaning. It is like a pearl within a bag whose light shines out through it:
the fool thinks the light belongs to the bag and discards it without taking [the pearl], while the wise person turns the bag inside out for him.
The purpose of revealing the jewel is to have it taken up and not discarded; this is its true intent. It lies solely in revealing the jewel—how could it lie in destroying the bag for lacking light?
The bag is like the eye, the light is like seeing, and the jewel is like the mind; this can be seen by reflecting upon it.
Thus, one merely reveals the nature of seeing and does not destroy the eye. Those who, on account of this, fall into the delusion of destroying seeing are yet another group of errors.
As for the third point: the Buddha said, "Although this vision is not the wondrous, brilliant, and pure mind, it is like a second moon—it is not a reflection of the moon.

The intent of these words was originally not a term of disparagement; rather, it was a slight suppression of the small to exalt the great, intended to encourage people to recognize it and not discard it.
Although he said it is "not the wondrous, brilliant, and pure mind," he slightly suppressed it because the preceding passage had already...
To call this "the essence of the clarity of seeing" means that the two characters "clarity" (jing) and "brilliance" (ming) are already inherently present.

It is because its substance (*ti*) is extremely subtle that it is called "refined" (*jing*); it is because its function (*yong*) is eternally profound and numinous that it is called "bright" (*ming*).

However, because within this substance there still persists the two kinds of inverted, deluded views which have not yet been eliminated, its clarity and brilliance are not yet sublime; therefore, it is said that although it is not yet the "sublime clarity and brilliance."

This merely indicates that [the faculty] has already attained clarity and brilliance (*jīngmíng*), yet lacks only one "subtle" (*miào*) quality; it is briefly suppressed for this reason, not as a profound disparagement.

However, the intent behind this slight suppression is to clarify that after one has recognized [this state], one must still eliminate delusions so that the clarity and brilliance may advance to the ultimate subtlety.
It does not mean that there is a separate "subtle clarity and brilliance" apart from this. As stated below:
Regarding the statement that "the second moon is not a reflection of the moon," this immediately clarifies the great distinction. For the second moon is not separate from the substance of the moon;
it is merely a semblance produced by pressing [the eye], unlike the third "moon in water," which is truly a hollow reflection and lacks substantial reality.
This further demonstrates its superiority over the preceding "consciousness-mind" (*vijñāna-citta*), for the latter is precisely like the [first] water.
The moon is empty and not substantial. Thus, within the metaphor, the moon has no distinct substance; when pressed, it becomes a second moon, and when released, it becomes the first moon.
There is no difference between one substance and one reflection. In the Dharma, the mind has no distinct substance;
when accompanied by delusion, it is the "essence of clarity in seeing," and when delusion is removed, it is the "wondrously clear essence-mind. There is likewise [no difference].
The distinction between the one that is real and the one that is false is intended to be fully grasped so that there may be no doubt.
Only by understanding it in this way will one grasp the true meaning of the Tathāgata’s words; for at this moment, he intends for Ānanda and the others to recognize this very seeing as the mind.
Various masters have failed to comprehend this intent; as soon as they see that it is not explicitly stated in the literal text, they immediately proceed to explain it away in various ways.
This is delusion. It seems as though there is a separate reality apart from this; thus, the ancient commentaries mistake the real for the delusory and mistake manifestation for refutation.
Furthermore, they say: "Because one perceives the manifest mind, although mind and perception mutually manifest each other, the primary manifestation resides entirely within the mind.
Thus, they mistake the single essence for two distinct essences. Fourth, when the Buddha clarifies that the two kinds of seeing are delusory, it is because [they arise] from within the faculties.

The seeing-nature (*darśana-bhāga*) is the very substance of the *ālayavijñāna*. Yet, this sutra refers to it as the subtle *ādānavijñāna*, while the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* calls it the *tathāgatagarbha-citta*.
Because it is a fusion of the true and the false, those of shallow intelligence are either deluded into thinking it is not true, or they are deluded into thinking it is purely true;
for this reason, the Buddha did not habitually expound upon it. Now, through his unobstructed great compassion, this sutra leads those following provisional teachings into the ultimate reality.
At the beginning, [the Buddha] took pity on sentient beings who were deluded regarding this nature as being non-authentic;
thus, following the refutation of consciousness, he exerted his utmost effort through ten rounds to reveal it as authentic, so that they might recognize and accept it without failing it.

At the end, fearing that sentient beings would become deluded by taking this nature to be purely authentic, he then briefly presented two forms of falsehood after the revelation of the truth, demonstrating its—
It is not the true. This causes one to awaken and break through it, so that one does not remain dormant or submerged in it.
Thus, the true is first revealed, ensuring that one does not mistake the true for the false; subsequently, the false is eliminated, ensuring that one does not cling to the false as the true.
In this way, one is doubly liberated from the two delusions of "true" and "not-true," such that the subsequent act of breaking through does not obstruct the prior revelation of the true.

To show: As for the old commentaries, because they later provide a brief refutation, they consequently obscure what was previously most clearly revealed, and judge it all to be a refutation of false views.
This is ultimately falling into the delusion of non-reality; it is a profound betrayal of one's own spiritual nature.
Is this not yet another great error? Thus, throughout a thousand years, these various masters have shared but a single glimpse of the nature of seeing.
In some cases, the headings and explanations do not correspond; in others, the mind (*citta*) and seeing (*darśana*) are analyzed as two distinct entities.

Consequently, the refutation and revelation appear unsettled, making it difficult to rely upon the distinction between the true and the false. All such instances have these four delusions as their root.
Now that the reasons for each have been clarified and the roots of doubt have been uprooted, the principle that "seeing is the mind" can be taken as definitive and free from uncertainty.

Ah! Only when one understands this in its entirety will one know that the destruction of consciousness is thorough and decisive as to its being false, while the manifestation of the faculties is ultimate and decisive as to their being true.
There must be no lingering hesitation or dualistic indecision. Yet, one still does not know how this relates to *śamatha* and the other [practices].
One must explain this point in order to clarify the reason why consciousness is destroyed and the faculties are manifested.
However, this was already briefly set forth previously within the *Śamatha* section of the "Questions and Answers on Delusion.

Now it is restated once more precisely because, through the wondrous *śamatha* and so forth, one clarifies that the essence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is inherently present by nature, whereas consciousness lacks such inherent concentration.

Alas, since practitioners stubbornly cling to their views, it is necessary to exhaustively refute them so that they may abandon [their attachments]. While the faculties possess inherent concentration, alas, practitioners...

Because they are entirely deluded, it is necessary to manifest [the truth] to the utmost so that they may grasp it. Furthermore, one should know that the employment of consciousness (*vijñāna*) versus the employment of the sense-faculties (*indriya*) is the basis for the distinction between the provisional and the real.
That is to say, to mistake consciousness for the mind and to hold that there is no mind other than this is the provisional teaching.

To realize that consciousness is not the mind and that there is a separate true mind is the real teaching. Question: There are many causes and conditions for distinguishing the provisional from the real; how could it be...?
Is it solely due to the distinction between the functioning consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the functioning faculties (*indriya*)? Answer: This is the division between the provisional and the ultimate.
Even if there are many conditions, the mind is their totality. If the mind is correct, then nothing is not correct; if the mind is not correct, then nothing is not incorrect.

Furthermore, since beginningless time, sentient beings have taken the entire nature-ocean of the Dharma-realm and deludedly transformed it into an ocean of consciousness, and then further transformed that ocean of consciousness.

The "seven waves" arise; these are precisely the aforementioned seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*). Among these seven, it is solely the sixth [consciousness] that moves the body and initiates speech.
Therefore, ordinary beings and followers of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) are not only deluded regarding the ocean of nature and the ocean of consciousness, failing to understand both;

furthermore, among the aforementioned seven evolving consciousnesses, they fail to recognize the existence of the seventh above, and below, they fail to discern the first five. They merely calculate...
The sixth [consciousness] exists because it is the characteristic of one's own mind.

When a Buddha appears in the world, does he not simply wish for every person to awaken to the fact that the preceding seven consciousnesses are not real, thereby directly fathoming the ocean of consciousness to restore the ocean of nature?

However, alas, sentient beings have accumulated delusion from delusion throughout kalpas as numerous as dust motes; thus, they cannot be awakened to instantaneously. Therefore, at the assembly of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, he spoke directly...
Dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is itself the arising of nature (*dharmatā*). This clearly demonstrates that the ocean of consciousness is itself the ocean of nature.

Yet, while the followers of the Two Vehicles sit in the assembly, they are like the blind and the deaf; how much more so for ordinary worldlings? Even the Buddha can do nothing for them but must directly accommodate their capacities by deriving provisional means from the ultimate reality.
Without correcting their mistaken perceptions, he follows their errors to lead them, guiding those of the human and heavenly realms and the Small Vehicle.
In the teachings, only the six consciousnesses are established as "mind. Therefore, among the seventy-five dharmas of the Hīnayāna, mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) constitute only a single category.

Nevertheless, the functions of this mind can be briefly divided into five types: first, the unwholesome; second, the wholesome; third, the imperturbable; fourth, those with minor fruits; and fifth, those with great causes.
Thus, for those who are unable to suddenly awaken to the ocean of nature, the Buddha [teaches] solely based on these distinctions of the mind.
Its application is to transform [the mind] gradually, progressing from the inferior toward the superior.

First, one teaches the vehicle of human beings and the vehicle of the devas of the desire realm, temporarily transforming the evil of this mind to lead it toward goodness, so that they may leave the suffering of the three miserable realms and obtain the happiness of humans and devas.
Second, he teaches the vehicle of the devas of the two upper realms, temporarily turning back the scattering and movement of this mind to cause it to return to the immovable state,

thereby enabling them to leave behind the inferior karmic rewards of the lower realms and attain the superior karmic rewards of the upper realms. Third, he teaches the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas,

temporarily turning back this mind’s attachment to existence so that they may awaken to and enter the principle of emptiness, thereby enabling them to leave behind the obstacles of the three realms of existence.
They realize the small fruits outside the [true] realm. Fourth, the Initial Teaching of the Mahāyāna is established:

for the time being, one turns this mind away from its attachment to the Hīnayāna, causing it to dedicate itself toward the Great Vehicle, so that they may abandon the small fruits and establish the great cause.

Using the essence of wisdom and concentration of the provisional Mahāyāna teachings, they still employ the six consciousnesses; that is to say, they take the mind of arising and ceasing as their fundamental cause for cultivation. Although they transform the *ālayavijñāna*, in the end—
There is no real fruit [to be attained]. Therefore, from the Āgamas onwards and prior to the Prajñāpāramitā, all [teachings] provisionally employed this consciousness as the "mind";
thus, they were entirely subsumed under the provisional, and everything was unreal. This is what is meant by "the mind is not [real], and there is nothing it does not deem unreal.

It was only at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* that the previous provisional vehicles were collectively discarded, and the single teaching of ultimate reality (*ekayāna*) was established. However, at that time...
At the beginning of the reform, considerable effort was required to sever doubts and engender faith; there was no leisure for a detailed discussion of the two minds of provisional and ultimate truth.
One merely removed the names of the three vehicles and abolished their provisionally granted fruits.

Since this scripture follows the *Lotus Sūtra*, great doubts have already been dispelled and correct faith has been established; one must now, however, reform the mental activities associated with those provisional vehicles.
He bestows upon them the essential heart-essence of the Perfect and Real. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "What you should now do is solely seek the wisdom of the Buddha. This is precisely it.

Therefore, at the very beginning of this scripture, the refutation of the consciousness-mind (*vijñāna-citta*) is the reforming of the mental activities of the provisional vehicles. The revelation of the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*) is the bestowing of the essential heart-essence of the Perfect and Real.
If the old commentaries were to openly attempt to rescue [the consciousness] at the point where it is refuted, they would forever solidify the mind of the provisional vehicles.
[The text] proceeds. Regarding the locus of manifest vision, those who are deluded and treat it as the refutation of views block and sever the perfectly real heart-essence of the school.

By simultaneously deluding both the refutation and the manifestation, the sublime purport of this sutra becomes entirely obscured and indistinct. If this is so, by what means can the definitive right faith of sentient beings be established?
And from where shall the clear eye of the Way open? It was for these unavoidable reasons that this new commentary was composed. This...
If one further examines this through the systematic analysis of establishment and refutation, the meaning will be fully exhausted.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the nature of the faculties revealed herein is the very source of the ocean of consciousness; it is not different from the ocean of nature (*dharmatā-samudra*), yet it is merely accompanied by ignorance.
Just as when the two fingers are pinched, sentient beings cannot perceive their nature if they abandon this [practice]. Therefore, this reveals the nature of the sense faculties (*indriya*).
It is not merely a primary point at the beginning of the sutra; rather, from beginning to end, the entire sutra takes this as its essential meaning.

Thus, when it is revealed, it is opened through the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*); when one enters into cultivation, one enters through the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*). All Buddhas, with one voice, agree on this.
It is taught that the cycle of birth and death, liberation, and nirvana are all identical to these six sense faculties and nothing else.

The verse concludes: "The *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) is subtle; its habitual tendencies form a torrential stream. Fearing that one might confuse the real with the unreal, I have never openly expounded it.
Now, the *ālayavijñāna* is merely another name for the consciousness of karma. If so, how could the wondrous nature within the sense faculties be a coarse or superficial phenomenon?
Alas! It is simply because the subtle and true essence is conjoined with the delusive habits of the torrential flow.

If one were to expound it, it would be necessary both to reveal its truth and to refute what is not true; yet those of shallow intelligence, upon hearing this, would inevitably fall into doubt and confusion.

Since it is difficult for them to awaken and easy for them to become lost, it is better that it remain unexpounded at all times. Now, this sutra is intended to lead those who follow provisional means into the ultimate reality. It does not...
Having attained it, he then expounded it in its entirety. The first ten sections most thoroughly reveal the Truth; the subsequent two views briefly refute that which is not the true fruit.

However, various commentaries fail to grasp this and are utterly confused regarding the revelation of the True. They generally label [the text] as "refuting the false" and "revealing the True," yet since there is no fixed distinction between the True and the False, they ultimately lack a reliable basis.
Consequently, regarding the Views and the Mind, they cannot decide whether they are identical or different. Thus, it remains unresolved.
All have fallen into the delusion of what is not true, and thus ultimately dare not recognize it as the mind.
How could the prophetic declarations of the Sage contain even a hair’s breadth of falsehood?
Third, summarizing the concise to indicate the extensive: At the beginning of the sutra, the two aforementioned delusions were briefly raised;

yet these constitute the greatest and most essential points of the sutra’s intent, and they remain entirely unclarified. As for the other various distinctions, whether major or minor, how could they all possibly be set forth?

Regarding those matters in the commentary that are easily understood, I have silently and privately corrected them without further debate; those with discerning eyes may distinguish between the clear and the turbid (the pure and the impure).
I myself also have points where right and wrong are confused, which cannot be left unaddressed in silence. I shall clarify these in this commentary, summarizing the major points:

such as the error regarding the "hanging hand" and "upright-inversion," the fallacy concerning the five stages of returning to the source, the mistake in the progression and regression of clarity, the doubt regarding the non-passage through *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, the sudden arising of the lack of distinction in the continuity [of consciousness], and the [explanation of] the three subtleties and six coarsenesses.

This is a confusion. Regarding the four meanings and the three baskets (Tripitaka), there is no point of return; regarding the two definitive meanings, they have not been reached. These do not transcend the two fundamental roots mentioned previously.
To seek the source of the fetters separately—how could one know that this is precisely failing to comprehend the six sense faculties?

The two characters "knowledge" (zhi) and "vision" (jian) are not merely explained directly as the six faculties; furthermore, the commentary text falls into the partiality of emptiness versus existence, or truth versus falsehood, while the verse text is simply false.

The simultaneous negation of both emptiness and existence—how could there be such a correspondence between prose and verse? "The six being resolved and the one perishing" follows the sequence of "unfurling and tying.
Not only is the individual response unclear, but while the Buddha’s words possess a sequential order, the commentary lacks it;
failing to realize that the vertical discourse is not horizontal, how could there be a single intended meaning in both the sutra text and the commentary? This is the twenty-fourth error.
They divide [the teachings] into great and small, and cling horizontally to their own notions of shallow and deep.

Regarding the nature of hearing within the faculty of the ear, they not only fail to understand it as the very mind of the preceding Three Piṭakas, but they have also failed to clarify the three emptinesses and the six knots.

They understand only the details of the "Three Determinate Meanings" regarding the precepts, yet they do not realize that the samādhi and wisdom of the site of enlightenment are precisely the perfect penetration of the faculty of the ear. Sentient beings are thus inverted.

One knows that karma is formed through the fetters of views and thoughts; thus, the world is inverted. One does not know that by distancing oneself from defilements, one draws near to the realization of the fruit.
Furthermore, it is because one abandons wisdom and adheres to attachments that suffering is produced.

Regarding the three gradual stages, one fails to understand that they merely involve the addition of precepts, yet remain within the ten minds prior to the stage of Perfect Penetration (*yuan-tong*). Thus, one falsely rejects the commentary of Mount Gu-shan.

This is erroneous; it is not the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*). It has not yet clarified that the ten minds are precisely the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) and the five powers (*pañcabala*). The ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*) fully bring one into birth within the Buddha-family;

the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) do not transcend the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*); how could the ten transferences (*daśa-pratipatti*) go beyond the three stations? The four stages of added effort (*catasraḥ prayoga-bhūmayaḥ*) are the non-duality of mind and Buddha;

the ten grounds (*daśa-bhūmi*) are merely the manifestation of the rational nature (*dharmatā*). All of these differ from the interpretations of the old [commentaries] and are not identical to them. This is all... [his].

The general intent of this major section is as follows. As for the remaining differences in structural divisions and the variations in wording and phrasing, they are truly beyond exhaustive description;
these must be discerned through the broad observation of the wise, who will surely leave nothing unilluminated.

One should know that the purpose of composing this layered commentary is to lament the overgrowth of weeds obscuring the Buddha’s intent and to take pity on the ignorance and blockages of later students, feeling a profound sense of不忍 (unable to bear) in keeping such truths secret or stingy.
Although I am aware that I have ultimately failed to repay the grace bestowed by the Buddha, I have nonetheless disregarded censure and ridicule to compose this commentary once again.
It is not that I dare seek fame or indulge in arrogance, nor do I wish to forcibly distort right from wrong to bring upon myself the long-term affliction of birth and death.
I hope that those who understand me will form a profound resonance with me, and those whose minds accord with mine upon a single glance will grant their seal of approval.

As for those of lofty intelligence who hold divergent views and do not entirely agree, I pray you will kindly instruct me without being sparing of your guidance. Having thus concluded my presentation of my own understanding, I shall now discuss the second point:

"The Ancient Models of the Dharma and the Extraction of the Great Outline. This refers to following the precedents of the ancients regarding the Dharma and extracting the great structural outlines from within the sutras. To examine this in detail, as follows:

Throughout the five periods since the Buddha’s coming, he established the teachings, which comprise an infinite variety of Dharma gates and an infinite variety of causes and conditions, ranging from the depths of their underlying principles to the differences in the capacities and faculties of sentient beings.
Now, in explaining this sutra, if one does not clearly understand these preliminary distinctions, one will likely be confused by the aforementioned matters. Therefore:
To provide a preliminary overview before the commentary is a fixed methodological principle.

However, following the various masters of antiquity, many compose ten topical divisions (*daśamukha*) prior to the commentary to set forth the sequence of titles; these are for the most part similar, though not without slight differences.
Therefore, although this enumeration follows the ancients, the sequence and titles are in fact not entirely identical; each is merely according to what [the author] has perceived.
1. Determining the time of teaching; 2. Categorization within the Pitakas and Vehicles; 3. The causes and conditions for its production; 4. The delimitation of its principles and meanings; 5.

The capacities of the audience for whom the teaching is intended; 6. The essence of the teaching as the expressive medium; 7. The general and specific purports of the doctrine; 8. The structural analysis.
Citation. Ninth, explaining the title according to the general commentaries; tenth, separately interpreting the meaning of the text. Regarding the first [point], determining the time of the teaching:
this is because various masters, due to the accounts transmitted in one or two distinct individual scriptures, found them to be somewhat inconsistent, and thus, regarding this sutra...

Diverse theories abound and the determination of the timing [of the teachings] is unsettled. Since the timing has not yet been fixed, it is difficult to distinguish between the provisional and the real;

furthermore, matters such as the arising through causes and conditions, and the inclusion within the various *piṭakas* and teachings, cannot all be definitively established. Therefore, we first establish the timing of the teaching at the outset.
Once the timing is settled, the distinction between the provisional and the real becomes clear, and there will be no further hesitation regarding the classification of the various categories.
Generally speaking, when times are separated by vast antiquity and lands are divided by distant regions, their historical accounts are often impossible to verify with certainty.
In this very region alone, how many matters are there that cannot be relied upon—where past and present differ and local corruptions have led to conflicting traditions?
How much more so, then, regarding the time and place of the Buddha in the Western Heaven, which are separated by such extreme distances; yet one seeks to reconcile these discrepancies...

To prepare a Sanskrit version in order to seek the truth of the textual evidence—is this not difficult? Therefore, regarding those historical accounts that do not coincide, one should cast them aside rather than clinging to them.

As for the original texts of the sacred scriptures, their profound majesty is manifest; they draw upon the wisdom of external sages and have been translated with meticulous completeness, such that the words and meanings are crystal clear.
If one relies solely on these to distinguish between the provisional and the ultimate, and to determine [the measure of] authority...
When the Dharma is taught, there is nothing that cannot be understood through the mind; how, then, can King Udayana and his son alone serve as an objection?

Now, based on the explicit and definitive meanings within the sutras: Ānanda sought the Buddha-way by means of the Two Vehicles, while Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra held that the cessation of an Arhat is itself Bodhi.

There is no restriction of five distinct natures; yet, some harbor doubts that [the teaching] existed prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and even descended into the *Vaipulya* and *Prajñāpāramitā* periods.

This implies that before the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, there was already no lingering attachment to the "transformed city" (the *śrāvaka* vehicle), and it was permitted that all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) would attain Buddhahood.
When the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* was preached, what further expedient means (*upāya*) remained to be opened, and what further [truth] remained to be revealed?
How truly manifest this is! How much more so when it is explicitly stated that Yaśodharā has already received her prediction?

If it were not for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* Sūtra appearing first to grant her this prediction, at what other time would she have received it? Furthermore, its appearance is solely for the sake of knowledge and vision;
only the Buddha exhaustively realizes the true reality (*bhūtārtha*). Prior to this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the śrāvakas had not yet been granted such an explanation. This sūtra...
The true aspect (dharmatā) is threefold; its emergence, knowledge, vision, and designation are fourfold.

If this were prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, then since he had already frequently preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* to the śrāvakas before this point, how could it be said that they "heard what they had never heard before"? The meaning of these passages is clear and manifest;
thus, it can be seen without doubt that they belong to the period after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Yet, masters such as Zhìyuán classified them as being within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Between [this life] and nirvana, one must necessarily see that they are identical in this regard. How can one recklessly disparage them based on such trivial matters as historical traces?
Some may say: "The Lotus Sūtra merely serves to harmonize and integrate those of the two vehicles who cling to provisional means and are deluded regarding the ultimate reality;
therefore, it is entirely directed toward the capacity of the two vehicles, and does not mean that prior to the Lotus Sūtra there was no real Mahāyāna meaning whatsoever."
Regarding these teachings—such as the *Vimalakīrti*, the *Śrīmālādevī*, and the *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras—all discuss the principle of the Buddha-nature as truly eternal.
Since they all predate the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, how can one know that the *Śūraṅgama* is not of this same category?
Thus, when various masters classified it as a Vaipulya-Prajñā text, it was certainly not without basis. Why must you reject their view and definitively classify it as a *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtra?

Regarding the period after that: the answer is that prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, although there were not entirely no teachings of reality (*satya-dharma*), it had not yet been explicitly granted that Śrāvakas could cultivate the Great Vehicle to attain Buddhahood.
Therefore, the Śrāvakas did not merely dare to publicly request to cultivate for Buddhahood; likewise, the Tathāgata did not openly proclaim the essential truth to them.
For this reason, Bodhisattvas repeatedly raised the censure of them being "spoiled seeds," and those of the Two Vehicles constantly harbored [doubts].
This is the pain of severed parts; thus, although the *Vaipulya* and *Prajñāpāramitā* [teachings] were actually complete, their provisional [expedient] aspects had not yet been revealed.

It was only upon reaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* that they were permitted to advance and cultivate the path to universal Buddhahood. Consequently, Śāriputra and the others recounted their sense of having previously heard nothing of this.
This can be verified by examining the text. Now, this sutra is identical to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* in that it takes śrāvakas as its primary audience.

Thus, what is requested by Ānanda and Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra are all the wondrous gates of the perfect and true reality; and what is expounded by the Tathāgata and the bodhisattvas are entirely the essential truths for attaining Buddhahood.
How could such questions and answers exist within the Vaipulya or Prajñāpāramitā [sūtras]? If one were to forcibly categorize it according to the Dharma...
Prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the Buddha had already granted permission for śrāvakas to abandon the Lesser Vehicle and cultivate the path of the Buddha.
Yet, upon reaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, why did Śāriputra say, "You only teach the bodhisattvas and do not speak this Truth for us"?
He felt deep personal grief at having lost the Tathāgata’s immeasurable knowledge and vision, further lamenting that from the time he first followed the Buddha, he had never heard such [a teaching].

This is what has been said. For what reason is it stated thus? Even if one were to employ clever words and convoluted defenses, it would ultimately be difficult to reconcile [this] with the time of Yaśodharā’s prophecy.
Therefore, this sutra is definitively situated after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*;
only then will the various meanings mentioned above not be in contradiction. May students refrain from excessive doubt and simply rely on the interpretations of the masters such as Zhìyuán.

It is judged to be correct. Question: Although the father and son, King Nimi and [his son], are not sufficient grounds for [this] mudrā, the King Nimi is present at the beginning of the sutra while Vairōcana has already fallen by its end.
How can this single period of the sutra be so excessively long? It is only natural that the assembly should have doubts and remain undecided.

Please do not cast it aside. I shall provide an analysis for you to uproot the root of your doubts. [The opponent] replies: "The ancient masters have already stated that the sutras were not delivered in a single assembly;
rather, they were compiled over different times and gathered into a single collection. This alone is sufficient to sever all doubt, so why trouble yourself with so many questions?
Furthermore, between the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, eight years elapsed. During such a long interval, what matter could remain unchanged? Moreover, King Bimbisāra..."
Being at the end of his life, how could this have been during the Buddha’s early years? It must be after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, perhaps seven or eight years later.

How could the rebellion of Virūḍhaka not have been concluded by then? However, the two assemblies for the compilation of the scriptures were merely designated as such; they never specifically pointed out the location [of this event].

Now it is suspected that it occurred after the scriptures had been finalized, when Ānanda requested the discourse on the seven destinies (*sapta-gati*) and the Tathāgata himself spoke of the five māras.

The location is entirely similar to what is explained separately in the later assembly. By using the three names of the preceding Great Samādhi to respond to the five titles of the Sūtra, the concluding textual structure forms a continuous chain;
how could it be interrupted? As for the seven destinies and the five māras, these are distinct meanings external to the Sūtra itself.
If one were to treat this as a separate assembly at this point, the distinction would indeed be clearly evident in the text. However, regarding King Bimbisāra and his son—
Doubts are likewise dissolved like ice melting away. Regarding the classification and inclusion within the two *piṭakas* (collections):

since the time of its teaching is after that of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is the supreme flavor of *tīrāma* (clarified butter), surpassing the two types of *ghṛta* (butter). Thus, what difficulty could there be in discerning to which *piṭaka* and teaching it belongs?

Nevertheless, the ancient masters maintain that when discussing the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) expounded by the Three *Piṭakas*, one should follow the primary [teaching] rather than the incidental, and adopt the majority [of the evidence].

Without taking even a small portion [of other categories], this sutra elucidates the training in concentration (samādhi-śikṣā), the Vinaya elucidates the training in ethical discipline (śīla-śikṣā), and the Śāstras elucidate the training in wisdom (prajñā-śikṣā).
Since this sutra discusses great meditative concentration extensively, it primarily elucidates the training in concentration.

Although there are minor elements of the ethical discipline for initiating practice and the wisdom of doctrinal discussion, these are merely ancillary and not the primary focus. Thus, one should know that among the Three Baskets (Tripiṭaka), this sutra belongs to the Sūtra-piṭaka.

As for the two *piṭakas*, they definitely belong to the Bodhisattvas and not to the Śrāvakas, because the practices requested by those suited to the teaching are exclusively those of the Bodhisattva path.

Furthermore, although it includes the exposition of dhāraṇīs and mantras and the title "Abhiṣeka" is designated, the manifest texts concerning awakening, cultivation, and realization exceed the esoteric ones by more than tenfold;
thus, it merely uses the esoteric to assist the manifest, rather than being the secret treasury itself.
This is a summary. If one takes this to encompass that, all other cases may be understood by extension.

As for why the Śrāvaka vehicle is also included, it is because the Śrāvaka precepts are not discarded and because there are minor differences in terminology. Regarding the inclusion of vehicles, it refers strictly to the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) of the Shared Teaching.
It also belongs to the One Vehicle of the Distinct Teaching (*bīja-śāsana*). If this [One Vehicle] subsumes that [Distinct Teaching], then the three and the five are both encompassed.

For instance, from the four grave offenses and the three gradual stages up to the causes and effects of the seven destinies, all are manifested; it does not even exclude the human and celestial realms, let alone the other vehicles.

Among the twelve divisions of the scriptures, Changshui states that it is subsumed under the two divisions of *sūtra* and *vaipulya*. As for its inclusion therein, it is as previously explained. Within this, there is the *pitaka* (collection).

This is a summary intended to correspond with the *Awakening of Faith*, while the classification of the vehicles was established by Master Jun. Regarding that which is brought about by the three causes and conditions:

as we observe in the world today, whenever any single matter is undertaken, it must have a specific cause and condition; how much more so for the Great Teaching of the Buddha—how could it have come to be without a purpose?
An ancient master said: "Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, cannot be moved by minor causes and conditions, nor can it be..."

It cannot be moved by minor causes and conditions. The sūtras spoken by the Buddha are likewise. According to Chengliang’s (Zongmi) commentary on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, there are ten categories of causes and conditions;
a detailed examination of the conditions revealed therein largely accords with the intent of the "Sixfold Accomplishment" and other such principles.
These are already explained within the sūtra itself, so I shall not elaborate further here. Regarding the causes and conditions of the root sūtra as set forth by Changshui (Zixuan), there is...

There is a distinction between the general and the specific. Regarding the specific, [the tradition] largely follows Xianshou (Fazang). Although this interpretation of the general is the same as his, the specific details differ in many respects.
Now, as for the "general," it refers to all the Buddha’s teachings. Generally speaking, they are intended to repay causes, respond to requests, reveal principles, and deliver sentient beings.

The principle revealed therein is precisely the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, which all sentient beings equally possess; yet, being deluded, they do not know it themselves, and thus they sink into birth and death. The Buddha, regarding...

Because he awakened to this within the causal stage and made the vow to attain Buddhahood in order to manifest it universally, the various teachings of the five periods—though they speak of provisional and ultimate truths and of varying degrees of clarity and speed—are primarily intended for this one great cause and condition.
This constitutes the general cause and condition for all teachings. Specifically, there are also ten [reasons]: first, because of the ultimate abolition or establishment [of doctrines]; second, ...

First, it is for the purpose of knowing and seeing; second, it is for the purpose of severing delusive views; third, it is for the purpose of manifesting the true mark (*dharmatā*); fourth, it is for the purpose of transforming the view of permanence;
fifth, it is for the purpose of leading one into the Buddha-wisdom; sixth, it is for the purpose of demonstrating true samādhi; seventh, it is for the purpose of directly pointing to the human mind.
Eighth, because it simultaneously demonstrates two gates; ninth, because it most earnestly exhorts toward actual realization; tenth, because it strictly guards against perverse thoughts.
It should be understood that these ten gates are entirely different from the causal conditions previously established by Changshui Yihai.
Regarding the first, the ultimate abandonment and establishment: although the *Lotus Sūtra* speaks of abandoning the provisional, it merely abandons its three [aspects].
Regarding the names of the vehicles and the characteristics of the fruits they permit, it clarifies that there are neither three vehicles nor three fruits.

As for establishing what is real, it likewise clarifies that there is only the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna), universally permitting the cultivation of Buddhahood and the attainment of Buddhahood, without further restriction by dividing them into the "Half" [Vehicle].
When it says, "All of you are Bodhisattvas," this merely confers upon them the designation of the Mahāyāna.
Thus, as long as the mental activities of the three vehicles have not been transformed, it cannot be said that the provisional has been ultimately discarded;
and as long as the essential core of the One Vehicle mind has not been bestowed, it cannot be said that the Real has been ultimately established.

This is precisely because the doctrines settled over forty years were suddenly overturned, causing people's minds to be thrown into turmoil and their webs of doubt to multiply. Therefore, I provisionally shattered [the former teachings] so that they might briefly attain faith and understanding. Now, [I shall proceed further...]

Furthermore, I have exhorted you with all my strength to circulate this teaching in order to stabilize your resolve; therefore, that previous sutra did not have the leisure to minutely eliminate mental activities or separately bestow the essential points of the mind.
It was only upon reaching this present sutra that I could finally bring to completion the reality of its definitive establishment and provisional rejection.
This is because, although there are many varieties of distinction between the provisional and the ultimate, the mind employed therein serves as the fundamental practice.

The "cause" (hetu) is the essential point of their differentiation. Therefore, throughout the beginning, middle, and end of this sutra, it repeatedly provides definitive judgments regarding the provisional and the real.
The minds employed by these two types of practitioners differ greatly; [the sutra] causes them to resolutely abandon the provisional and take up the real.
As the initial judgment states: "All sentient beings, in the continuous succession of birth and death, do so entirely because they do not know."

The eternally abiding true mind employs various deluded thoughts; thus, all sentient beings—including those of the provisional and limited vehicles—continue through the cycle of birth and death, sharing the same category as those subject to transformation.

Therefore, one should know that "deluded thoughts" refer to the minds employed by those of the provisional [vehicles], while the "eternally abiding true mind" refers to the mind employed by those of the ultimate reality.
This remains somewhat obscure and requires further explanation for clarification, which will be provided later.
The analysis of these two kinds of fundamental natures is now perfectly clear and requires no further supplementation or explanation. The text states:

"All sentient beings possess the seeds of karma naturally; yet practitioners fail to achieve unexcelled Bodhi, even descending to become provisional, Hinayana, demonic, or heterodox followers, all because they do not know these two kinds of fundamental natures and practice in a confused manner—just like boiling sand in an attempt to make rice."
For kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, nothing has been accomplished. First is the root of birth and death, which is that攀緣心 (pān-yuán xīn) [the攀緣心]—the攀緣心—that you now employ as your own nature.

This refers to the 識心 (shí-xīn) [consciousness-mind] to be refuted below; it is that which you must cause to be abandoned, thereby repudiating the false root.
This refers to the fundamental nature. To cause one to employ it is to bestow the true foundation.
It is a pity that the old commentary fails to understand that the "true foundation" is precisely the seeing-essence (*darśana-viśuddhi*) pointed out below;

this is because the old commentary uniformly identifies the locus of seeing as being entirely a false vision to be destroyed. If one carefully examines the meaning of the Tathāgata’s analytical discourse, then...
To know why all those who employ provisional means do so is to understand that it stems from their taking the deluded mind as the fundamental cause for their practice.
If these [provisional means] are not refuted and made to be abandoned, then the Lotus Sūtra would merely have the empty name of "provisionality" while the mental activities remain unchanged;
they would continue as before to steam sand in an attempt to make rice. How could this be ultimately abandoned? This is truly why people...
Regarding "being real": it is because one can take the nature of the faculties as the fundamental cause for cultivation.

If one does not grant [the teachings] so that they may be employed, then although the *Lotus Sūtra* would merely establish the name "real," the ordinary mind would not employ it; consequently, there would ultimately be no real fruit.
How could it be established as ultimate? Upon reaching the section on the two definitive meanings within the *Samādhi*, it follows the previous [text].
There are two [types of mind]. Those that should be discarded must certainly be discarded; those that should be adopted must certainly be adopted.

However, the "first determination" simultaneously encompasses both the meanings of discarding the false and employing the true. As for the statement that the mind of birth-and-death which has been discriminated cannot serve as the fundamental cause for cultivation, this refers precisely to the aforementioned consciousness-mind that clings to objects;
moreover, the text below explicitly states that one must first select and discard the mind of birth-and-death.
The "root of death" is precisely the root of departing from delusion. Yet, regarding the preceding passage on names and words, not even a hair’s breadth has been altered.
The old commentary, unable to briefly illuminate the Buddha’s words, arbitrarily adopts the proximate text and explains it as the karmic function of the five turbidities.

Furthermore, that [passage] instructs one to rely upon the nature of the non-arising, non-ceasing, perfectly湛 (zhan) [profoundly still] essence; this is the application of the true source. However, the old commentary again separately explains this as the three types of cessation (*śamatha*).

This contemplation has no connection whatsoever with the preceding text; consequently, it causes the realization and cultivation [of the path] to fail to form a single coherent sequence, leaving later students forever lost.
As for the second determination, it merely requires one to resolve upon using the authentic text while adding further detail.

Furthermore, the subsequent passage cites the testimony of all Buddhas to prove that the nature of consciousness is empty and false, like flowers in the sky; both birth-and-death and nirvana are nothing but the sense-faculties.
As for their natures, when it comes to the selection of the perfect organ of liberation (*pariśuddha-vimokṣa*), they ultimately employ only the faculty of hearing.

This is precisely how the provisional mental practices of individuals are transformed, and the true foundation of the perfect reality is bestowed. One should know that the Tathāgata’s primary purpose was to ultimately abolish the provisional and ultimately establish the real;
therefore, he preached this sūtra. As for the specific designation of "cognition and vision" (*jñāna-darśana*), it is generally based on causes and conditions.
Although it is said that all teachings possess [this truth], the provisional schools are merely concealed and indirect discourses, not explicit explanations.
It is only from the *Lotus Sūtra* onward that there are explicit teachings. Yet, at the very beginning of this revelation, one could only dismantle names and titles;

there was no leisure for a precise and detailed indication. The reason for this lack of leisure has already been explained in the preceding text. Consequently, the various commentators each followed [their own interpretations].

I shall explain this according to my own understanding. If one takes the three knowledges (*trividya*) and five eyes (*pañcacakṣus*) as constituting "knowledge and vision," then one speaks solely from the perspective of the fruit-stage virtues (*phalaguṇa*).

This fails to examine in detail how the Buddha’s discourse on "opening, showing, awakening, and entering" contains both meanings: that which is inherently endowed (*prakṛtistha*) and that which is accomplished through cultivation (*bhāvanā-samudāgata*).

When ancient masters explained this, they mostly adopted only the meaning (*artha*) without carefully following the literal phrasing (*vyañjana*). If one were to rely entirely on the meaning and not the phrasing, [the text would remain obscure].
This would result in the sacred word possessing only the unimpededness of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*) while lacking the unimpededness of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*).

How could this be acceptable? Now, according to the text of the sutra itself, it says: "Because one wishes to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddha-jñāna-darśana*), so that they may attain purity;
