By providing a detailed analysis of the five māras, he alerts them to external māras who lie in wait, admonishing them not to indulge in false interpretations that would invite such calamities. He further elucidates the latent māras within, admonishing...
Do not give rise to false awakenings that lead to such provocations. Finally, it is reiterated that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are nothing other than delusive thoughts (*vikalpa*).

From beginning to end, one is cautioned against perverse thinking. Thus, we know that the Tathāgata preached this sutra to strictly guard against such perverse thoughts. Synthesizing the ten preceding meanings, the treatise states:
"To investigate the abolition and establishment [of teachings] is to transcend the provisional and enter the real; to open up knowledge and vision is to [realize] one's own mind."

This is precisely the Buddha. To realize the true mark (*dharmatā*) is for all phenomena to be identical with the mind; to understand that marks are eternal is to see that fundamentally there is no arising or ceasing.

To enter the Buddha-wisdom is for the fruit to be ultimately perfected; to attain true samādhi is to be free from the toil of grasping. To point directly at the mind is to personally behold one's original reality;
to clarify the two gates is for nature and cultivation to be without obstruction. To aspire toward actual realization is not to stop halfway; to guard against the heterodox...

If one contemplates this, it will never be destroyed. Thus, while the first four and the sixth and seventh [sections] most clearly manifest the inherent nature (*xingju*), the fifth and the final three [sections] indirectly accomplish the perfected cultivation (*xiucheng*).

Yet, every stage is the supreme definitive meaning (*liao-yi*) of the Perfectly Real School (*Yuan-shi zong*). This is truly what is called a most magnificent cause and condition; how could it be compared to those trivial, meaningless words that merely pursue each section in isolation?

Let those with discerning eyes savor this. [Note: The original Chinese text contains a typographical error: "節節" (jie-jie) appears twice, but based on the context of the *Zongjing Lu* and the structure of the text, the second instance is likely intended as "節節" (jie-jie) referring to the stages of the text.]

The section on causes and conditions is concluded. Regarding the fourth point, the "Delineation of Meanings and Principles" (*yili-fenzi*): "Meaning" (*yi*) refers to the substance of the text; "Principle" (*li*) refers to the master of the matter.

Furthermore, meaning is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), while principle is the essence (*svabhāva*). Accordingly, when the Sage established his teachings, he unified them through principle and analyzed them through meaning.
Although principle is ultimately one, it becomes shallow or deep according to the capacities of sentient beings; although meaning results in multiplicity, [it is nonetheless subsumed by principle].

Yet, when returning to the underlying principle, there is no separate essence. Thus, since the meanings and principles of the various sūtras possess varying degrees of depth, if one who elucidates the sūtras does not distinguish between them, how can they know the limits of their respective scopes?

That which this ocean of sūtra-meanings follows is precisely the entire text of the *Qixin lun shu* (Commentary on the Awakening of Faith). Now, Master Xianshou was a world-renowned patriarch who truly deserves veneration; however, he—
Since the text is already complete, why labor to record it in its entirety? It is sufficient to provide a brief account that points toward the full scope.

That [explanation] has two aspects: first, regarding the breadth or narrowness of the teachings; second, regarding the arising of the dharmas. Within the section on the teachings, there are five stages proceeding from the shallow toward the deep. First, regarding the Hīnayāna teachings:

they speak solely of the emptiness of the person (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), relying only upon the six consciousnesses and the three poisons. Second, regarding the Initial Teaching of the Mahāyāna: this refers to the School of Emptiness (*Śūnyavāda*).

There is the obstructive non-manifest (avijñapti), which is also called the "partial teaching" (*fenjiao*). "Partial" means limited. This refers to the Characteristics School (*xiangzong*), which holds that some beings do not attain Buddhahood.
Third is the "final teaching" (*zhongjiao*), which subsumes the initial under the final; it teaches that the *tathāgatagarbha* follows conditions to become the *ālaya-vijñāna*.

It maintains that not only is everything empty, but all things are also suchness (*tathatā*). It is also called the "real teaching" (*shijiao*), for it sets aside the provisional to reveal the real, teaching that all sentient beings...
All shall become Buddhas. Fourth, regarding the Sudden Teaching (*dun-jiao*): it holds that only the nature (*xing*) is without marks (*xiang*), and there is no gradual progression;
it reviles teachings and abandons thought, asserting that "the mind itself is the Buddha. Fifth, regarding the Perfect Teaching (*yuan-jiao*):

it unifies the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), wherein nature and marks are perfectly interfused, such that bodies, lands, atoms, and hairs are mutually and repeatedly inclusive. This is but a brief citation; the details are found in those texts. If one were to clarify [this] among the five...
The scope of this sutra refers to the faculties and natures indicated within the scriptures; it encompasses the four categories and seven elements as their fundamental substance.
This is the *ālayavijñāna*—another name for the *tathāgatagarbha*, the *tathatā* that evolves according to conditions (*pariṇāma*) and constitutes the subtle *ādānavijñāna*.

While ordinary beings undergo defilement, those of the Lesser Vehicle who turn toward the Great Vehicle shall all attain Buddhahood; this precisely belongs to the ultimate truth of the final teaching.
This teaching belongs to both the Sudden and Perfect teachings, as cessation is itself Bodhi and it perfectly illuminates the Dharma-realm.

If one classifies the sūtras according to the teachings, these five [sūtras] are subsumed under the latter three teachings; if one classifies the teachings according to the sūtras, then this [teaching] can fully encompass those five.

This is because it does not discard the fruits, dharmas, and precepts of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) teachings, while simultaneously preserving the eight consciousnesses and the three emptinesses of the Initial Teaching (Śrāvakayāna).

Second, regarding the arising of phenomena, there are likewise five stages of increasing depth as one proceeds from the fundamental to the derivative; however, that which is being discussed here is as follows:

Regarding the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna* (Dasheng qixin lun), its classification likewise does not depart from the five teachings; it merely distinguishes them from the previous section by proceeding from the profound to the shallow.
First, "taking the single mind as the source" refers to the one true dharma-realm (*eka-dharmadhātu*), which encompasses all four dharma-realms;
this is the scope of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). Second, "based on the single mind, opening two gates" encompasses the [first] two teachings. The single mind...
The gate of True Suchness (tathatā) is the scope of the Sudden Teaching. Within the Emptiness school of the Initial Teaching, this gate is also taught implicitly.

Second is the gate of the Arising and Ceasing of the Mind, which is the scope of the Final Teaching. Third, based on the latter gate, two meanings are clarified: first, the meaning of awakening; [second, the meaning of non-awakening].

Second is the meaning of non-awakening. Based on the latter of these two meanings, the three subtle states arise: first, the phase of karma (*karmalakṣaṇa*); second, the phase of transformation (*pravṛttilakṣaṇa*); and third, the phase of manifestation (*ābhāsalakṣaṇa*).
This constitutes the scope of the *lakṣaṇa* school within the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*).

Because that school does not realize that these [three subtle states] and True Suchness (*tathatā*) share a common source in the One Mind, it asserts that True Suchness does not allow for following conditions (*pratyaya-anuvartana*). Thus, the arising of phenomena is limited to the level of the *karmavijñāna*; even when it transforms, [it remains so].
Wisdom is likewise ultimately conditioned and thus not identical with the Truth. The five [stages] depend on the final birth; these are the six coarse factors: first, the distinct objective sphere;

second, the arising of sensation; third, attachment to sensation; fourth, conceptualizing names; fifth, the performance of karma; and sixth, the experiencing of retribution. This concludes the third section: the limits of the Minor Teaching (*kṣudranikāya*).
Fifth is the distinction between humans and devas; this too is cited here only briefly, as the full details are found in that text.

If one were to clarify the depth and shallowness of this sutra among these five categories, the text would show that it explains both the true and the false in an integrated manner, wherein the false is reconciled back into the true, and the false arises from the true.

When one examines in detail such [teachings] as the harmonious fusion of the true and the false, it is generally seen that they are equivalent to the "Gate of the Arising and Ceasing of the Mind" (心生滅門) and do not contradict the aforementioned scope of the Final Teaching (終教).

If one further investigates and realizes that the false, having been integrated, all returns to the nature of wondrous True Suchness (妙真如性), then they also coincide with the "Gate of the True Suchness of the Mind" (心真如門) and likewise do not contradict the aforementioned inclusion within the Sudden School (頓宗). From...
Since reality (*tattva*) arises from the three subtleties and six coarsenesses, this clearly aligns with the Mind of Arising and Ceasing (*citta-utpāda-vyaya-mukha*) as its ultimate, actual meaning.

However, since the union of reality and delusion reaches its subtle perfection within the mind of the four dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*) and the three Tathāgata-garbhas, it also concurrently aligns with the mind of the single original source.
Furthermore, this does not contradict the previous principle of the simultaneous integration of the perfect and the partial.

Thus one knows this sutra. When its meaning is measured and its analogies drawn, it is nearly on the same footing as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Awakening of Faith*, and the *Avataṃsaka*—sharing the same category and thread.
It is a most profound and unsurpassed scripture, yet it is represented by the *Buddhoṣṇīṣa*; how supreme it is! The section on the "Delimitation of Meaning and Principle" concludes.

Regarding those sentient beings reached by the five teachings, one must distinguish between the universal, the common, and the restricted, thereby performing the inclusion and exclusion. Simply seek...
One must constantly exclude those who are not of the right capacity; this refers to the selection of those who are the appropriate recipients.

As for the universal application [of the teaching], it is based on the ultimate intent of the *śāstra* teachings, which clarifies that all sentient beings who possess a mind shall all attain Buddhahood.
Since this sutra explains the method by which one achieves Bodhi, what person would not be included among those to be benefited? As the sutra says: "All sentient beings, from..."
Since beginningless time, the continuity of birth and death has arisen entirely from not knowing the eternally abiding true mind and instead employing various deluded thoughts.
Furthermore, it is said that for all sentient beings, the seeds of karma naturally cluster like the *akṣa* fruit;
and that practitioners who fail to achieve Bodhi, even becoming Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, gods, non-Buddhists, or Māras, do so because they do not know these two [truths].

The two fundamental roots, such as the confused practice [of cultivation] and so forth—inferring from this, does the Buddha’s mind not universally desire that sentient beings employ their true mind to abandon delusive thoughts, thereby exhausting the two fundamental roots? Question:
If there is no discrimination in this regard, would those sentient beings who do not believe or comply with it also be subject to it? Answer: There are precedents; they too would be subject to it.
It is also like the case of the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging, who forcibly bestowed predictions upon those who were unfaithful and disobedient;

even though they fell into hell due to their slander, it nevertheless became for them the causal condition for the *Lotus Sūtra* over distant kalpas. Thus, there is not a single person who is not a suitable vessel for this sūtra.
This is the ultimate state of universal penetration. Why, then, would there still be any limitation or partial application?
Although the cultivation of life through this universal penetration is vast, when discussing its benefits, they are for the most part distant causes and conditions rather than immediate benefits.

If one were to accept only those instances where the benefit follows hearing and the faculty and principle accord like the simultaneous pecking and hatching of a chick and a hen, then one must necessarily limit oneself to these cases and cannot allow for indiscriminate inclusion.
Furthermore, within this there are two ways to understand [the meaning]: first, by examining and verifying the text; second, by inferring through one’s own reasoning.
First, regarding the examination and verification of the text: Ānanda is the primary interlocutor (*pratimukha*) for this sutra, and he is thus situated at the level of a Śrāvaka.
Yet, if one carefully examines how the Tathāgata describes his actions at every stage, it is clear that these were mostly intended to guide those of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) toward conversion.

The small enters the great. As the Sūtra says: "You should first cultivate revulsion for and detachment from all the Hinayana teachings of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and resolve to diligently seek unsurpassed Bodhi," and so forth.
Within this, there are four categories; the first is the Śrāvaka who is still in training (śaikṣa).
The Sūtra says: "Out of compassion for Ānanda and all those in the assembly who are still in training (*śaikṣa*).

It further says: "Also so that those with outflows (*āsrava*) in the future may attain the fruit of Bodhi. This refers to the first category. Second, it is for the Śrāvakas beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). The Sūtra says:

"Addressing Pūrṇa and all the Arhats in the assembly whose outflows were exhausted and who were beyond training. This refers to the second category. Third, it is for both [categories] together as conditions.
"Awakening. This refers to what the Sūtra says: "Out of compassion for those among the assembly who are pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas whose bodhicitta is not yet sovereign.
These four are all of fixed nature. This refers to what the Sūtra says:

"To cause those in your assembly who are śrāvakas of fixed nature, as well as all those arhats who have not yet attained the two kinds of emptiness and have not turned toward the Mahāyāna. Question: Those of fixed nature will certainly not believe.

Question: Within the selection [of those to be gathered], how are they categorized? Answer: Those within the present assembly who, according to their invitations and listening, do not ultimately withdraw from their seats;

therefore, they are also the proper recipients of the teaching. Indeed, because these followers of the Hīnayāna have suffered through kalpas, yet found no essential means for seeking liberation, and have engaged in successive, clumsy practices with immeasurable toil and hardship—this is what most moves the Buddha’s compassionate pity. How much more so when their wisdom is superior?

Regarding the "remnant dust" (those who follow after): throughout successive lifetimes, they have been born together with the Buddhas and have mostly been their close kinsmen; how could it be only Ānanda?

Observe the title of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, which speaks of "rescuing and protecting one's own kin"—its intent is evident therein. Because they were recently reached by the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, they have only now come to know and seek faith;
thus, these individuals clearly represent the primary objects of the teaching. As for those inferred by means of reason: although the sūtra does not explicitly state this directly...

Pointing this out, I shall infer by means of my own understanding: when a follower of the Hīnayāna first turns their mind toward the Mahāyāna, the Buddha still repeatedly expounds for them the gateway for entering the Great Vehicle.
However, as for those who possess purely great faculties and are entirely devoid of the seeds and habitual tendencies of the Hīnayāna, the Buddha must certainly act even more profoundly for them.
It is only because he seeks to urgently rescue those of small faculties that he first speaks of the Small Vehicle at each stage, while simultaneously acting for the sake of the Great Vehicle.

The intent [of these passages] is contained within all of them. As the Sūtra says: "I now establish for you the great Dharma-banner, and shall also cause all sentient beings throughout the ten directions to obtain the wondrous, subtle, and esoteric [teachings]," and further:

"And for the sake of sentient beings in the final dharma period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, I cause them to resolve upon Bodhicitta and open the path of wondrous practice of the Unsurpassed Vehicle."
It further states: "It shall also serve as the cause for world-transcendence and as the eye for all sentient beings of the future.

Since it repeatedly mentions "all sentient beings" and again specifies "those who resolve upon Bodhicitta in the final age," one knows that this is not intended solely for the single class of the Hīnayāna, but extends equally to ordinary people of great resolve and those who have entered the stages of the Initial Teaching (Śrāvakayāna). This...

In the middle [category], one should possess six types. That is to say, two belonging to the provisional vehicle and four belonging to the perfect and real. Regarding the two of the provisional vehicle:
these refer to those of the Mahāyāna Dharma-lakṣaṇa school, who constantly cling to dharmic characteristics and are unable to integrate essence and appearance;

and those of the Mahāyāna Prabhākara (Destruction of Characteristics) school, who encounter the term "non-existence" and fail to realize the wondrous nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*. These individuals precisely lack clarity regarding this.
"Having passed through ten great causal conditions, how could one not take what is correct as the perfect and ultimate reality?

This refers to those ordinary beings of superior capacity who, furthermore, lack the seeds or habitual tendencies of the provisional vehicles and rely solely on the Supreme Vehicle to resolve upon Bodhicitta. Their faculties are even more pure;

it goes without saying that the Buddha’s teaching is directed precisely toward them. Question: Since they already know that the provisional and small [vehicles] are not the truth, they purely resolve upon...
"Great mind" need not be laboriously broken down or revealed; what benefit does this sutra provide for such a person? Answer:

Since they are called "ordinary beings of superior capacity," it is clear that although their resolve is great and their aspiration is universal, they have not yet attained the essential key to awakening or the subtle gate of realization.
This sutra points directly and demonstrates both the equal causes and conditions; is this not precisely for them? This...

Within this, there are four categories: namely, those who possess three faults while lacking one fault. Those who possess faults are the three types of persons mentioned previously in the ninth section on causes and conditions:
first, those who rely on the empowerment of others; second, those who rely on hearing and neglect meditative concentration; and third, those who rely on their innate nature and forget cultivation.
The one who lacks faults is one who does not possess the aforementioned three faults. Although they seek empowerment, they apply themselves to personal practice.
Realization: Although he possesses extensive learning, he remains constantly in meditative concentration; although he has awakened his nature, he practices with extreme refinement.
Lacking only final, penetrating awakening to enter this most supreme and foremost wondrous faculty, he is one who is perfectly suited to the occasion.

If he hears this sutra, it will truly be like timely rain nourishing the grain or the spring thunder leaping the carp—nothing can resist its power. Although this is the most excellent, when combined with what precedes it—
These five types are all those for whom the Mahāyāna is appropriate. Formerly, regarding the first five [categories], it was held that they were all excluded as being unsuitable vessels;

yet this fails to recognize that, based on explicit statements, the two vehicles are clearly and manifestly the very ones for whom the teaching is intended—so how could those of great capacity conversely not be suitable vessels?

If one were to exclude them through a biased diagnosis of their "illness," then this sutra would be precisely the medicine to cure that illness; how then could the vessel and the teaching not correspond? If one were to avoid the illness...
I did not dare to treat them. How could I call this a "good medicine" when it fails to address the profound ailments of the Two Vehicles, which still pose such danger?
Yet, how much more so would a single dose suffice to cure the slight ailment of the Mahāyāna?

Therefore, the reason the Sūtra explicitly describes the Two Vehicles as its primary audience without clearly designating the Mahāyāna is precisely to demonstrate that if it can treat even those who are difficult to cure, there is no need to mention those who are easy to cure.
Thus, including the preceding, there are ten categories in total, all of whom are those suited to the teaching.

Furthermore, while Avalokiteśvara personally recounts his own past practices, Mañjuśrī likewise expresses their shared cultivation. As the verse says: "The Tathāgatas of the past have already perfected this gate;
the Bodhisattvas of the present now each enter the perfect clarity; those who practice and study in the future should rely upon such people as these. This is so.
Thus, the Mahāyāna of the three periods universally relies upon this as its correct standard; yet the ten categories are not particularly numerous.
This concludes the discussion on the capacities of the sentient beings to whom the teaching is addressed. Sixth, regarding the essence of the teaching that expresses [the truth]:

Master Xianshou’s commentary on the *Awakening of Faith* briefly establishes four gates, while Master Qingliang’s commentary on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* expounds ten gates, which likewise do not exceed the opening of those four. Changshui composed the *Yi* (Meaning) on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Master Hai also followed Xianshou’s abbreviated approach; I shall now likewise follow that brevity and list those four gates.

First is the gate of following characteristics (*xiāng*). This, according to Changshui, is further divided into two: first, taking only the substance of the expressive [words]. This refers to sound, name, phrase, and sentence.

The provisional and the real support one another and cannot be discarded in isolation. For while the Buddha was alive, he resided in sound; after his passing, the teachings on paper and ink consist of names, phrases, and sentences.
It is manifold. Nevertheless, it also relies upon the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) and together constitutes the substance of the teaching; it is not limited to sound and so forth alone.

Since the substance of that which is expressed (*vācya*) arises from the conjunction of the two [word and meaning], mere words without meaning do not constitute the teaching. Only when word and meaning follow one another and are not separated does the substance of the teaching come to be established.

Second is the gate of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), which subsumes the aforementioned objects because they arise from the mind. This also has two aspects: first, the correspondence between the original and its reflection (*mūla-pratibimba*).

This means that the teaching as the essence consists of the words and meanings manifested by the pure consciousness of the speaker, while the teaching as the reflected image consists of the appearance of the aspects of those words and meanings within the consciousness of the listener.

It should be understood that both the speaker and the listener fully encompass these two aspects. Qingliang (Chengguan) inherited and expounded upon the four propositions concerning the relationship between the original and the reflection, thereby dividing the teachings into four categories:

namely, the Hīnayāna (Small Vehicle) is solely the original; the Initial [Teaching] is both original and reflection; the Final [Teaching] is solely the reflection; and the Sudden [Teaching] is neither.
Furthermore, according to the teachings received, the exposition that fully incorporates the eight phrases divides the teaching into two categories:

the inclusion of the sentient being and the Buddha within one another belongs to the *samāna-śāsana* (teaching of commonality), whereas the distinct presence of the sentient being and the Buddha belongs to the *viśeṣa-śāsana* (teaching of distinction). This intends to reveal that when they are perfectly interfused without mutual obstruction, it alone constitutes the profound *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).
Regarding the section on the nature of the Three Refuges, Xianshou alone maintains that this consciousness has no substance other than True Suchness (*tathatā*). Thus, the subsequent text states:
"All phenomena, from the very beginning, are free from the characteristics of verbal expression... ultimately they are but the One Mind; therefore, they are called True Suchness.
Qingliang cites the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* to explain that the teachings flowing forth from the "superior stream" of True Suchness are the most excellent.
Therefore, I say that the Pure Name is called "non-existent. To speak of liberation while transcending words is also the intended meaning of this gate.

Regarding the Gate of the Four Unhindered Knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*), Xianshou states that within these preceding three gates, mind and objects, principle and phenomena, share a single *paratantra* arising;

they are fused without obstruction, mutually penetrating and encompassing one another, thereby constituting the essence of the teaching. This is because the Dharma of the One Mind has two gates, each of which...

Because it encompasses all phenomena (*sarvadharma*). I maintain that the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*) subsumes the "conformity to characteristics" (*lakṣaṇānuvartana*) aspect of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), while the gate of suchness (*tathatā-mukha*) first subsumes them back into their fundamental nature (*dharmatā*).

Thus, the former gate establishes the non-obstruction between mind and objects (*citta-viṣaya-avyāghāta*), and the latter gate establishes the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*li-shi-avyāghāta*).

Qingliang (Fazang) inherited and expounded these two gates of non-obstruction—between principle and phenomena, and between phenomena and phenomena—and ultimately returned them to the Sea-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*).
The samādhi also reaches the ultimate limit of the principle of non-obstruction; it is simply subsumed under this present sutra.

Now, since this sutra properly belongs to the final and ultimate [teaching] while simultaneously encompassing the Perfect and Sudden, it accords perfectly with all the categories of the essence of the teaching as judged by Xianshou and Qingliang.

This concludes the discussion on the essence of the teaching that expresses [the truth]. Regarding the seventh point, the general and specific characteristics of the "purport" (zongqu): Xianshou explains as follows:
That which is venerated by a particular school is called its "tenet" (zōng). That toward which a tenet tends is called its "orientation" (qù).

Qingliang took "tenet" to mean that which is esteemed within a discourse, while his "orientation" was the same as Xianshou's. Both masters possessed both the universal and the specific gates; the universal refers to the one great teaching of time.
"Local" (jú) refers to taking only this specific sutra; "universal" (tōng) refers to comprehensively applying it across all teachings.

There are many ways to open the gates [of analysis], so I shall not cite them at length. Now, I will simply take them according to the general intent. As for the teachings of the five periods, the provisional and the real can be briefly distinguished.

Provisional vehicles are largely formed through cultivation; they extensively unfold cause and effect, such that the cause is itself the essence (zōng) and the fruit is itself the destination (qù). This is the Perfect Realization (yuánshí).
The "Endowment with Multiplicity" begins by clarifying awakening and entry; thus, awakening is the essence (*zong*) and entry is the goal (*qu*).

If this sutra were to be understood in general terms according to the class of teachings on perfect reality, its essence would likewise be the clarification of the ground of mind through awakening, while its goal would be the realization and entry into the ground of fruition.
This also roughly exhausts the general outline. However, the two masters [Zhiyi and Zhanran] were restricted to their respective schools.

The meaning is likewise vast and extensive. Now, restricting ourselves to this sutra, we shall extract its textual meanings according to the intention of Master An [Huiyuan], briefly presenting a small portion thereof.
One must distinguish between the general and the specific. The general refers to taking perfect concentration as the primary tenet and the ultimate fruit as the goal.
This is because that which Ānanda requested—wondrous *śamatha* and so forth—is precisely the Tathāgata’s teaching on the three *tathāgatagarbha*-minds.
The nature of true, perfect, and harmonious great samādhi—is this not the primary tenet of this sutra?
Ānanda requested that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions attain Bodhi, and the World-Honored One, summarizing and indicating, led them into the Tathāgata’s wondrous sea of adornment:
"To fulfill Bodhi is to return to non-attainment. Is this not the ultimate, final fruit of the Buddhas of the ten directions? Is it not indeed the primary tenet of this sutra?
"Where does it lead? [The questioner] asks: "What distinguishes this from the cause and fruit of the provisional vehicle? [The respondent] answers:

"The Great Samādhi shown here merely takes up what is inherently possessed (*xingju*), occurring entirely through the gate of awakening; furthermore, the ultimate fruit attained likewise selects only one wondrous gate—a direct, transcendent entry."

That which is called "that which is clarified by the clarifying cause" is not something produced by a producing cause; compared to the provisional vehicles, it is as different as heaven and abyss. Question:

What is the purpose of the subsequent passage on the sequential realization of the stages and positions? Answer: It merely reveals that perfect interfusion does not obstruct the progression through the stages;
it is certainly not a gradual realization over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. Have you not heard that those of sharp faculties accomplish the task in a single lifetime? Furthermore, the sutra...

End. After the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are destroyed, the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) is finally established. The Tathāgata clearly permits that from within the mutual functioning [of the sense organs], one transcends all stages.
One may see this for oneself by deeply investigating this meaning. If one were to elaborate further, there should be six pairs of distinct meanings:

namely, destruction and manifestation; partial and total; awakening and entry; essence and function; practice and stage; and differentiation and fulfillment. In each case, the former belongs to the fundamental principle (*mūla*), while the latter belongs to the ultimate destination (*niṣṭhā*). Furthermore...
All [teachings] tread upon the path of the former [part] as the basis for the latter part, and thus give rise to its path. First, regarding "refutation and manifestation":
taking the refutation of the consciousness-mind as the thesis (*zong*), the manifestation of the root-nature (*genxing*) is the path (*qu*).

To say that the refutation is exhaustive and detailed means that the intent lies in causing one to abandon the consciousness-mind and instead illuminate the nature within the six sense organs. Second, regarding "partial and total": partial...
Taking the fundamental nature (*mūla-prakṛti*) as the primary tenet, it fully reveals the Three Piṭakas as its ultimate aim.

This is precisely what is subsumed within the previous section on "Manifesting the Fundamental Nature," where it was first exclusively and variously clarified that the essence of vision (*darśana-bindu*) is perfectly wondrous.

The intention therein was to proceed from the proximate to the remote, fully revealing the four categories and seven elements (*mahābhūta*) as the Treasury of Emptiness, the ten delusions and three continuities as the Treasury of Non-emptiness, and the four meanings and three piṭakas as the Treasury of Emptiness.

This is the Amoghasiddhi-garbha. Regarding the three modes of awakening and entry: taking the complete realization of the jeweled hall as the primary principle (*zong*), and attaining the gate to enter deeply as the goal (*qu*).
This also follows from what was previously fully revealed regarding the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*); that is, the complete realization of the jeweled hall.

As for why one must necessarily seek the complete realization of the jeweled hall, the intention lies in attaining the single gate of the perfect faculty (*yuan-gen*) to enter the stream from the beginning, right up until the manifestation of *nirvāṇa*.

This is the preceding section. Regarding the four aspects of essence and function: taking the realization of the essence of perfect penetration as the primary principle (*zong*), and the manifestation of the function of perfect penetration as the goal (*qu*).
This also follows upon the previous gate to enter deeply and realize the essence of perfect penetration.

However, the purpose of necessarily realizing this essence lies in manifesting the thirty-two great sovereign functions of perfect penetration, such as the thirty-two transformations. Regarding the five aspects of the stages of practice: they involve the operation of the perfect...

Taking meditative concentration as the primary practice, one proceeds through the stages of the perfect cause as the goal. This also follows upon the previous summary of the great function of universal penetration and the correct, perfect concentration.
Furthermore, this summary has two aspects: first, the ability to benefit sentient beings; second, the ability to attain the fruit of Buddhahood.

While the preceding thirty-two manifestations primarily reveal the function of benefiting sentient beings, they implicitly encompass the function of attaining the fruit. Now, we speak of "operating the practice of perfect concentration."
This refers to the application of attaining the fruit. When it says "one must employ the practice of perfect concentration," the intent is to traverse all fifty-five stages of the perfect cause.
Regarding "the six parts being fulfilled," the primary principle is to traverse the stages of partial realization of sainthood, while the ultimate goal is to attain the perfection of Bodhi.
This also follows the stages of the perfect cause, which are precisely the stages of partial realization; thus, it says one must necessarily traverse these divisions.

As for the stage of realization (*sākṣātkriyā*), its intent lies in the fulfillment of unsurpassed bodhi. Reaching this occurs through awakening, which leads to entry; through entry, it becomes deep; and through depth, it reaches the ultimate.
Once one has proceeded along this path, it becomes clearly manifest before one's eyes. Thus, the sequential stages and their perfect integration are non-obstructive.

This concludes the section on the general and specific aspects of the fundamental aim. Regarding the eighth section, the citation of structural divisions (*ko-p'an*), this details how the ancients established these divisions.
To understand the scriptures thoroughly is the established method; it is like the compass, square, level, and plumb-line of Master Gongshu.

To abandon the structural analysis (*ko-p'an*) of tens of thousands of words of scripture and instead follow the literal text, explaining them in a diffuse and unstructured manner—how is this any different from abandoning the compass, square, level, and plumb-line while attempting to achieve squareness, roundness, levelness, and straightness?
One will likely never hit the mark. Generally speaking, there are four types of application. First, those that possess an original structural outline (*ko*), as provided by the primary expositor.

In the main body of the text, one should divide it according to its own internal structure, as in the cases of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), for which the scriptural passages are currently extant;

when interpreting them, one must follow these divisions. Second is the method of dividing by textual sections (*vibhāga-pada*): this refers to instances where the sentences are extensive and lengthy, such that if one does not carefully examine the flow of the text...
If one were to cut it up haphazardly, it would easily become disordered; therefore, the sections are divided from beginning to end so that the portions are distinct and do not overlap.
This may also be termed "dividing into portions" (*fenji ke*).

It is like a unified state divided into thirteen provinces, each province further divided into several prefectures, and each prefecture further divided into several districts and counties, proceeding from the broadest units down to the smallest.
Narrow [categories] develop into many from their origins, each possessing its own system of affiliation. Thus, by citing a prefecture or county, one knows to which department it belongs;
by citing a department, one knows to which province it belongs. Each has its own boundaries, so they do not become confused or overlapping.
However, these are not the original, fundamental divisions; rather, they were established by commentators based on textual evidence, as illustrated in this commentary.
This refers to the ten sections that clarify the nature of seeing and so forth. Third is the sectioning according to meaning (*yì*).

This means that regarding the meanings expounded within the text, where there are elements that correspond and should be combined—such as the categories of body and mind, pervasiveness, and the dependent and the primary—if these are not clearly evident in the text, they are divided according to their meaning to make them manifest.
For example, in passages such as "body and mind are vast and open," [the divisions are made based on the underlying sense].

This refers to the section on classification (*vibhāga*). Fourth is the section on sequential origination (*utpatti*). This means that the speaker explains the sequence in which the textual meaning arises according to the logical flow (*yukti*).
It is like a tree trunk: first there is a single root, which then branches into two, three, or four major limbs;
from each of these major limbs, various intermediate branches emerge, and from each of those intermediate branches, various minor branches emerge.
Even when reaching the smallest sub-section, one can still discern from which major section it originated.
If the commentary did not clarify its source, how could it be investigated? This is like Vasubandhu’s resolution of the twenty-seven doubts regarding the *Vajraśekhara*;
in the section answering the "Five Greats' Perfect Interfusion" in the root sūtra, the old interpretation completely loses the thread of the discourse and fails to connect with it.

Continued: The new commentary (*shū*) emerges to address its underlying doubts and adds a section on "Pulse Lineages" (*hakuroku*). Only then does one understand the intent behind [the previous work].
However, the composition of these lineages is most inappropriate; the generations are thrown into disorder. It is like a family lineage:
from one founding ancestor there may be three sons or five sons; the children born to each of those sons vary in number—some more, some less—and all of them are grandsons.
One generation must not usurp the status of its son; yet that which is born from a grandson is a great-grandson, who likewise must not usurp the status of his grandfather.

The masters of Tiantai, Xianshou, and Qingliang were able to exhaustively elucidate these subtleties. In recent times, works such as the *Yaojie* (Essential Explanations) and others are entirely ignorant of this principle;

within a single generation, they arbitrarily divide it into seventeen or eighteen sections, or even twenty or thirty, yet upon close examination of their divisions, [they reveal their lack of understanding].
In that case, the High Ancestor and his descendants—even down to the great-grandchildren—would all be ranked as a single peer group, entirely devoid of hierarchy or subordination.
What meaning, then, would there be in such a division? Now, I [the author] have drafted this work to remedy this defect;

the categories established herein are designed so that the great descend to the small, and the few increase toward the many. I fear that in ancient systems, one merely followed the order of the genealogical chart (*shū*) without assigning specific character titles (*mōji-gō*).
Distinguish them. However, many commentators are confused; they place the ten celestial stems and twelve earthly branches within circles and label them at the head of each section.
For instance, if "Jia" (甲) is the father, then "Yi" (乙) is the son; if "Bing" (丙) is the grandson, then "Ding" (丁) is the great-grandson.

This ensures that their respective generations are clearly manifest and do not become intermingled or disordered. At the conclusion of every major section, one should conclude by stating: "The [Name] Major Section."
This concludes [the section]. Thus, there will forever be no further labor of confusion or searching for categories. I earnestly request that future editors comply with this;
do not reject it as being unusual or unnecessary. There are four types of citations: first, sūtras and śāstras; second, the root sūtra;

third, the words of the patriarchs; and fourth, ancient commentaries. Within this commentary, in order to avoid prolixity, the sūtras, śāstras, and the root sūtra cited therein mostly consist of essential extracts.
In brief, the entire text is extremely concise; the words of the Patriarchs are likewise so.
As for the old commentaries of various masters, if they were found to be inconsistent with the Buddha’s intent, I would either remain silent and not follow them, or openly refute and correct them.
This was never done out of a deliberate desire to do so; rather, it was only done when absolutely necessary. Apart from this, I have preserved one [text] and discarded another.
Regarding the phrases that accord with the principles of the text, I shall certainly not dare to omit them, nor shall I dare to conceal them.

As for the mantras recited at the site of practice (*dojang*) to manifest the Dharma and bring benefit, as well as the passages concerning the twelve classes of beings and the ten habits and six intersections, since it would be cumbersome to labor over alternative explanations, I have taken these entirely from the commentaries of former masters.
All of these serve to clarify the titles and headings; the full texts are not... [repeated].
There are none. Furthermore, where there is complexity, those who have made slight reductions or omissions will certainly not damage the original intent.
At the end of a textual passage, if one adds further text from the original commentary, it should be separated by a circle (○) to distinguish them.
This concludes the citation of the topical outlines (*kōhan*). Ninth, the general explanation of the title; tenth, the specific interpretation of the text’s meaning. This—

I shall not trouble you with a redundant preface regarding these two gates; they will be presented when we enter the commentary. Following the ten gates of the ancients, I have merely set forth their headings.
Now, I shall further consolidate the preceding text to directly present the essential meaning of this sutra, thereby demonstrating its unique distinction from all other sutras and treatises.
It is explained here with particular clarity and intimacy. There are four points.
First, one must resolutely not employ the conscious mind, for it is a mortal enemy of Great Samādhi.

If sentient beings harbor even the slightest attachment or stinginess toward this [consciousness], they will ultimately never perceive the True Mind and Great Samādhi, let alone be able to accomplish them. Why is this? Because...
This consciousness falsely manifests the appearance of mind while in reality it is not mind; it falsely manifests the appearance of concentration while in reality there is no concentration.

Ultimately, through the exhaustion of obstructions, the true mind is revealed as fundamentally concentrated, yet it causes ordinary people, non-Buddhists, and those of the provisional or limited vehicles to be like those born blind.

Although other sutras and treatises also describe this as delusory, their words are general and brief, truly failing to reach the point where both good and evil are discarded, and both movement and stillness are transcended.
Because both [extremes] have been discarded: although sentient beings may hold base and inferior thoughts in contempt, they still value superior and wholesome thoughts;

though they may abandon the distracted consciousness, they still grasp at the consciousness of tranquil concentration. Since they cling entirely to the semblance, they certainly do not recognize the Real.
Yet the True Mind is fundamentally settled—how could it be seen? Only through this sutra does one awaken to the sound of the Buddha-dharma.
Since [the Buddha] still rejected these as unreal, how could he have retained the superior and wholesome mental application (*manasikāra*)?

Since he ultimately did not allow the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*) to be true, how could he have preserved the consciousness of tranquil concentration (*samādhi*)? It was precisely regarding this consciousness that he refuted it, until nothing remained.
Thus, the Buddha’s refutation of the mind did not take the time to discuss inferior and evil distraction; rather, he directly and specifically targeted the superior and wholesome [consciousness].

Those who abide in quiescent concentration break it; they fear that those practicing the Great Samādhi may be deluded by what appears to be right but is actually wrong, and thus ultimately fail to advance toward awakening to the True Mind’s fundamental concentration. Alas for people today!

Those who take stillness as their practice and the cessation of thought as their concentration have yet to be able to escape the narrow circle of this consciousness. They believe this concentration is easy to achieve.

Once the mind of seeking a worldly existence has arisen, how could one know that even with a hundred stratagems it is difficult to achieve during cultivation, and that what is achieved is ultimately not real?
It is like attempting to form crystal by freezing water; its difficulty and falsity can be understood by analogy.
I urge those who admire the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* to follow the Buddha’s words and swiftly abandon [such practices]; only then may they hope for the Great Samādhi.

Second, one must decisively recognize the nature of the sense organs (*indriya*). The nature of the faculties of sentient beings is itself the true mind (*tathatā-citta*) and is also the primordial stillness of self-nature (*svabhāva*).
This is because sentient beings have, through delusion, transformed the entirety of the *tathāgatagarbha* into the eighteen realms (*dhātu*).

Yet its actual substance resides within the six sense organs; the six objects (*viṣaya*) are merely reflections of the organs, and the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) are, in turn, reflections of the objects.

Sentient beings, on the contrary, identify with the most insubstantial consciousness-mind, while remaining entirely oblivious to their most substantial root-nature; there is nothing more extreme than this perversion.

Furthermore, while other sutras and treatises generally elucidate the essence, characteristics, names, and meanings of the true mind, they do not specify which among the bodies and minds currently present within sentient beings is that very mind.
Therefore, even if sentient beings were able to abandon their coarse discriminating mind, [they would still fail to realize the truth].
Furthermore, they frequently seek out profound and mysterious meanings and admire lofty, remote realms.
Consequently, they take their true mind to be a dark and unknowable state, characterized by a flickering and unstable appearance.

They may even investigate and contemplate with extreme precision to realize it, yet they remain as before trapped within subtle consciousness and flow into the provisional realms of the Lesser Vehicle, unaware of this.

I have now awakened to it. This very sutra points directly to the six sense faculties as the fundamentally pure essence of Bodhi and Nirvana—the state of blissful liberation, quiescent, wondrous, and eternal—without there being any other thing.
Furthermore, by snapping the fingers and flashing the light, the nature of seeing manifests clearly before us, unwavering;
and by striking the bell and inducing the dream, the faculty of hearing remains profoundly still, free from arising or ceasing.
Yet it remains ever-present; this is all demonstrated by pointing with one's finger, not merely through the exposition of words and phrases.

Moreover, when gazing upward at the sun and moon, they are clearly perceived across forty thousand *yojanas*, and when listening from afar to thunder, it is heard throughout more than three hundred *li*.

How much more so when the ten instances reveal the subtle and the three fingers point to the reality—it is truly extraordinary. If one were to withdraw these perceptions into the stillness of darkness, [the same clarity would remain].
As for the hearing within [this state], it is vast and boundless, encompassing the world-systems of dust;

all are the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of sentient beings, not dependent upon the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Furthermore, all forms are identical to the double wheel atop a lamp, and all sounds—

All are like echoes within the head; thus we know that the fundamental nature (*mūla-prakṛti*) is the substantial body of all phenomena, while all phenomena are but illusory reflections of that fundamental nature.
How could the true mind of profound mystery and ultimate subtlety ever depart from the ordinary nature of seeing forms and hearing sounds?
Although it is most proximate and most luminous, it is difficult to believe and difficult to understand therein; it is not because it is obscure and unfathomable.
It is simply because people do not realize what is used daily that the Patriarchs were unwilling to speak it through and the Tathāgata did not constantly expound it;
there is indeed a profound reason for this. Question: If it is so intimate and clear, why do the Buddhas and Patriarchs not constantly expound it and refuse to speak it through?

Answer: It is feared that those who are not of the right capacity would hear it and, whether they take it as true or untrue, both would fall into delusion. Therefore, it is not for the sake of those already deluded by what is untrue.

Those who hear this do not believe it to be true. They claim that while there are sentient beings who search in the dark for the profound and mysterious, they treat what is right before their eyes with contempt.
Upon hearing that the six sense organs are themselves [the Buddha], they assume that seeing forms is merely ordinary and that hearing sounds has nothing extraordinary about it.
Since they do not trust this thoroughly, they will certainly fail to recognize it. It is like Ānanda, who even after five fascicles [of instruction] still regarded them as separate.

Please examine the original source. The *Huikai* (Comprehensive Explanation) by the ten masters all regard the "manifestation" (*xianjian*) as that which is to be refuted. This is because they do not understand the primordial mystery (*yuanyao*) and the primordial luminosity (*yuanying*).

Is this not the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, which is fundamentally eternal and fundamentally quiescent? It should be known that this is precisely the wondrous mind of nirvana. One must realize this.
Apart from this nature, not even a fragment of a thing can be found; how could there be anything else mysterious or sublime?

When those who are truly deluded hear this, they rely on what they perceive as "true" and no longer apply themselves to cultivation. There are sentient beings who, relying on their own so-called "heavenly truth," do not seek ultimate realization;
upon hearing it said that the fundamental nature is already perfected, they either cling stubbornly to a silent and eternal essence or abandon all practice and verification.
[This is] a renunciation. Or perhaps one merely dwells in the initial understanding of the emptiness of persons and considers a small attainment sufficient;

not realizing that the root fetters have not yet been dissolved, how could one possibly escape the realm of emotions and transcend all suffering? With birth and death not yet extinguished, how can one transcend the realm of the physical world and realize perfect penetration?
This is much like guarding gold ore while content with poverty, or closing off the City of Transformation while remaining lost to the treasure. How could such a thing be permissible? For this reason—
Thus, both the true and the untrue constitute delusion; for this reason, the Buddhas and Patriarchs have never expounded upon them.

Those who fortunately encounter this scripture should quickly recognize their own fundamental nature and cease further seeking to unravel knots; only then will they have grasped the essential meaning.
Third, it is determined that the Tiantai *śamatha-vipaśyanā* is not employed.

This is because the various schools' designations for the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) were originally the Tathāgata’s revelation to sentient beings of the inherently existing true mind and its intrinsically endowed wondrous concentration.

He first pointed it out by means of the visual faculty, and it subsequently permeates all phenomena, causing one to perfectly realize that all existence is collectively the single nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*, thereby manifesting what was previously hidden.

Furthermore, since every person already possesses this wondrous essence of the *Śūraṅgama* from the very beginning, the text merely instructs them to awaken to and clarify this ocean of nature (*dharmadhātu*), serving only as the basis for the "entrance through perfect penetration" discussed in the subsequent sections. Originally, no system of meditative gates was established to teach formal cultivation;
yet, various schools have been muddled and arbitrarily imposed the "three contemplations" (*trividha-vipaśyanā*). Had the three contemplations been established from the outset, then...
The preceding passage fully explains the gate of cultivation. Why, then, does Ānanda later again request the analogy of repairing a magnificent house?
Could it be that this too merely illustrates the gate of cultivation and does not illustrate the nature of the treasury?

Furthermore, could the answer regarding "entering deeply through a single gate" mean that one enters deeply into that very gate of cultivation, rather than entering the nature of the treasury? All such [interpretations] are utterly untenable. One should know this.
The reason this sutra is so vastly different from other scriptures is precisely because its aim lies in the faculties (*indriya*).
The reason this concentration (*samādhi*) is so vastly different from all other concentrations is that it explains the fundamental concentration of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

If one were to claim that the preceding text describes the gate of cultivation (*bhāvanāmukha*) and thus entirely obstructs the concentration of intrinsic nature, then furthermore, it would hinder the wondrous cultivation of the ear-gate (*śrotra-dvāra*), rendering it useless.
Those who cultivate the Śūraṅgama Sūtra certainly do not employ the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*). Alas!

Having been practiced for so long, among those who study the Śūraṅgama, there is not a single person who does not search for the three contemplations; it seems they merely borrow the scripture as a "tile for knocking at the door."

It is precisely for the purpose of elucidating the *Tiantai* system of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. Ultimately, this ensures that the intent of the contemplation is uniquely clarified, and the obstacles to the intent of the sutra are completely removed.
How is it that such delusions, chronic ailments, and fragmented interpretations have reached such a state? It is right to thoroughly scrub and cleanse them away.
Question: The sutras and commentaries have been transmitted in this land for fifteen hundred years. Is it not the case that there has never been a single person who saw [the truth] as you do?
Yet you alone offer a divergent teaching that is truly startling. Fearing that many will be unable to believe it, what further explanation can you provide to comfort them?
Answer: The Great Master Zhiyi did not see [the truth] directly. Had he seen it personally, he would certainly never have erred in his explanation of *xing* (nature).
He taught the contemplations for them, yet he never presumed to be satisfied with his own views; rather, he looked up to the scriptures, seeing that they did not accord with his own.
Why else would he have sought [the truth] with an empty mind for eighteen years? Thus, the fault lies entirely in the confusion of later generations, while the Great Master has no part in it.
Qingliang and Guifeng each specialized in their respective works on the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Complete Enlightenment*.
I have no leisure to provide a detailed explanation here. As for the great adepts who realized the mind within the Chan school, it is not that they were unaware;

however, because the scriptural texts point so directly to the mind being within the sense faculties, there was a fear that this would become mere conventional worldly discourse, making it difficult to guide others.
Thus, such "perfectly complete" statements were especially avoided by those transmitting the lineage, and for this reason, many remained silent and did not speak of them.

Even if there were one or two instances of "picking up and holding" (nianti), they were picked up and then immediately swept away; in the end, they were never allowed to become formal exegesis or contemplation.
The intent of Lingyuan’s rebuke of Hongjuefan can be seen from this.

Furthermore, those who in antiquity expounded upon the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* did not necessarily, as is the case today, emphasize the three contemplations (sanguan) so much as to obscure the Buddha’s own words regarding the nature of reality. Therefore, my words are not necessarily entirely different [from theirs].
Regarding the ancients, it was solely because those of recent times have allowed their minds to be carried away by what merely resembles valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), leading to a chorus of errors;

thus, I alone have manifested my words as particularly distinct. How could I dare to evade the sin that fills the heavens? Question: Why does your commentary not avoid being circulated within the conventional world (*saṃvṛti*)?
Answer: There are two reasons for this. First, the teaching must be expressed through speech; this differs from the Gate of the School (*zongmen*). What cause for resentment is there?
It shall be disseminated. Second, as the autumn evening descends upon the patriarchal halls, there is no one left to receive direct realization through immediate perception (*pratyakṣa*).
What benefit is there in keeping it secret? It is better to reveal it so that it may pass through their ears and become a cause for realization.

This is the same intent behind the *pingchang* (commentaries) on the patriarchs’ final words, intended for them to be transmitted and practiced. Question: If direct realization through immediate perception cannot be achieved, what benefit is there in its transmission? Answer: It can enable...

For the most part, those of superior-middle faculties achieve true inference (*anumāna*) and give rise to great understanding, which serves as a preeminent causal condition for the realization of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Nevertheless, there may also be a small number of those with the highest-of-the-high faculties who achieve the realization of direct perception; this cannot be determined with certainty.
This statement is made because we are in an age of decline; had it been the ancient era of the School of the Patriarchs, [realization] would have come through hearing the sutras.
How could there be any limit to those who have attained awakening through this?

Fourth, one must decisively esteem the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*). Those who inquire into the *Śrī Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* and the *Śrī Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*—who among them does not know that this is the foremost expedient means?
Why, then, is it necessary to laboriously re-emphasize its importance? The answer is: what kind of statement is this? Since the flourishing of our own school in recent times...
Regarding the Three Contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*), everyone knows only to esteem them, claiming they constitute the correct cultivation of the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*.

Yet, while the commentators insert their efforts with great diligence and repeatedly clarify the teachings down to the section on the "Gate of the Ear," they regard it as a method for beginners and provide only a cursory explanation following the text.
Who has seen them conduct a profound research and extensive commentary upon it, or offer earnest exhortations for its exclusive cultivation?
"Ah! Furthermore, you say that everyone knows how to value this; you must have deeply penetrated its meaning. Try pointing out where the text of 'Perfect Penetration' (Yuantong) is.
The man laughed and said, "From the passage where Avalokiteśvara first speaks of 'within hearing,' up to the verse of Mañjuśrī’s selection, the scripture has explicit wording.
What difficulty is there in seeing it? He replied, "This is for those of inferior intelligence who follow [the literal text]..."
To speak of the knowledge that gives rise to understanding, how could one dare say it is not easy to perceive?

If one possesses the intelligence of an average person, they will know for themselves—from the latter half of the first fascicle, within the "First Determination of Meaning"—that the nature of the perfectly湛 (zhan) and unarisen-unextinguished which was inferred therein is precisely the nature of this faculty of hearing.
Furthermore, from the second meaning, where the knots of the faculties are pointed out and the perfect penetration is secretly selected, up to...
The passages concerning striking the bell to awaken from a dream, the Buddhas providing witness, and tying a cloth to demonstrate knots are all teachings on the nature of the faculties (*indriya*).
However, they do not explicitly clarify which faculty is most perfectly complete and should therefore be the sole object of cultivation.

This is what those of middling capacity understand. If there is further insight that penetrates through to the highest wisdom, one should know that after the destruction of consciousness (*vijñāna*), that which is shown is the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*).
This refers to the primary faculty of seeing as the fundamental basis for true cultivation.

Since seeing and hearing do not possess distinct essences, the tenfold manifestation of seeing is also the manifestation of hearing; thus, even within the discourse, the word "hearing" is included, as when Ānanda says:

"If this seeing and hearing are necessarily neither produced nor extinguished," and so forth. However, when the essence of seeing confronts objects, it clearly illuminates the myriad phenomena and remains eternally present.
The *amala* consciousness is immovable and easily awakened; therefore, it was emphasized in the preceding text. The nature of hearing is free from marks and hears throughout the ten directions;
it penetrates walls and passes through windows, making it most beneficial for the practice of mental integration. Therefore, it was specifically employed in the subsequent text.

Thus, we know that the passage from "Pointing out that seeing is the mind" up to "refuting [the view that it is] a combination of conditions" constitutes the revelation of the essence of the nature of hearing within the Perfect Penetration (*yuantong*). How could there be...?
Is it a separate entity? To speak at the ultimate level: prior to this passage, the initial refutation of consciousness is precisely the removal of the obstacle to perfect penetration.
If the mind of consciousness is not completely relinquished, one will certainly not know that there exists a separate root-nature;
and if one does not yet know the root-nature, how could one know from where to cultivate perfect penetration? Following this passage, the four aggregates and the seven elements...

Up to the third [section], the Tathāgatagarbha and the mind of the ten dharma realms, there is nothing that is not the ultimate measure of the root-nature (*indriya-gotra*); yet it is not that there exists a separate nature.

If one who cultivates *yuan-tong* (perfect penetration) does not realize this, how could they know that within "returning the hearing" (*fan-wen*), all phenomena are subsumed and the One True Reality is fully exhausted?
Generally speaking, the revelation of the inherently possessed *tathāgatagarbha* is precisely for the purpose of providing the foundation for the subsequent cultivation of *yuan-tong*.
It enters through the sense-base of the ear. Otherwise, what other dharma could the magnificent mansion entered through the subsequent gate be?

Thus, even before the Perfect Penetration (yuan-tong) was explained, these were all not outside the nature of Perfect Penetration; how much more so after it has been explained—could there possibly be any different dharma?
Therefore, the concentration and wisdom of the site of enlightenment (dao-chang) are undoubtedly this very [nature]. This is the third gradual reversal.
"Flowing and dispersing. This refers to the ten minds of the first abode; it clearly states that all are "perfectly penetrating" (*yuan-tong*).
Furthermore, even the equal and wondrous Bodhi is merely the ultimate perfection of penetration. The conclusion of the Contemplation of the Buddha states:

"All these are because of the three progressive advancements, whereby one is well able to accomplish the fifty-five stages. The meaning of this is evident: the phrase "three progressive advancements" merely restates the state of perfect penetration.
This is that sutra. The first half entirely discusses the *tathāgatagarbha* (store-nature), thereby revealing the perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*).
The second half entirely explains perfect penetration, thereby cultivating and realizing the *tathāgatagarbha*. From beginning to end, the entire sutra is for the sake of Perfect Enlightenment;

how could it be limited merely to the few words of Avalokiteśvara or the several verses of Mañjuśrī? Even the refutation of the five aggregates (*skandhas*) and the discernment of the five demons (*māras*) are still...

The Commentary on the Sections states: "To be far removed from perfect penetration and to turn one's back on the city of Nirvana—such is the essential core of this entire scripture, yet it is fully encompassed and exhausted by the three contemplations alone. How could I bear to remain silent and not speak? Question:

Since the Perfect Penetration is called a "convenient means for the beginner," there must surely be other methods beyond this that constitute profound cultivation. Why, then, do you say that these [three contemplations] exhaust [the teaching]?
Is it that from beginning to end there is no other dharma? This remains highly questionable. Please clarify the reason for this. Answer:
The various schools are all equally deluded in this regard, and your question likewise stems from the influence of long-standing habits; the root of doubt has not yet been fully uprooted.
I shall now uproot it for you. The reason lies entirely in the fact that the two characters "initial mind" (*chūshin*) have not had their counterpart clearly defined.

Yet they claim that the "initial mind" mentioned [in the sutra] refers to the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*), asserting that these alone constitute the profound Dharma. Consequently, they maintain that the initial mind of the sutra must necessarily be the initial mind of the three contemplations.

However, upon examining the enumeration of terms such as *śamatha* and so forth mentioned in the preceding section on the Buddha’s presence, one finds they merely coincide with the meaning of the *tathāgatagarbha*;

their characteristics are also similar. Thus, they conclude that these must indeed be the three contemplations, and based on this, they judge the preceding three baskets (*tripiṭaka*) [to be provisional].
The former [classification] requests the profound cultivation of the three contemplations at their deep stages as the "perfect penetration" (*yuan-tong*);
the latter classifies the initial entry of a beginner into a single gate as "penetration" for later students to follow, treating it as an established doctrine that no one dares to move.

This is not understood, for the former judgment falsely takes nature (*xing*) to be cultivation (*xiu*), while the latter demeans the deep to be shallow; moreover, the original intent is not clarified, and the sequence of the shallow and deep is lost.
This is a great error and is not a definitive argument. Herein I shall fully set forth the correct principle so that future students may never again be confused.
Now, the false attribution of nature (*prakṛti*) to cultivation (*bhāvanā*) has already been thoroughly clarified, leaving no aspect of the meaning unexhausted.

As for those who later disparage the profound as shallow, they fail to realize that the first three Tathāgatagarbhas, if considered according to the fundamental nature (*dharmatā*), are the ultimate source of all phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). For example:

In the vast emptiness of space, how could there be any distinction of depth or shallowness? If one considers those who attain realization herein according to their immediate capacity, it is unnecessary to debate whether their past roots were sharp or dull;

one simply takes the majority case. Within the six stages of the Tiantai school, these individuals mostly transcend the stage of "identity with principle" (*li-ji*) and reside precisely within the stage of "identity through name" (*ming-zi-ji*), because they have not yet entered the stage of "contemplative practice" (*guan-xing*). This continues until...

Regarding Perfect Penetration (*yuantong*), one proceeds from the stage of contemplative practice (*guanxing ji*), passes through the stage of semblance (*xiangsi ji*), and subsequently reaches the initial stage of partial realization (*fenzheng ji*).
According to this sutra, this corresponds to the manifestation of divine functions such as the thirty-two transformations.

According to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, it corresponds to the attainment of enlightenment through emanated bodies within the worlds of a hundred Buddhas. Compared to the previous stages, how different is this—like heaven and abyss! Yet now, [you] conversely...
If one claims that [the latter] is inferior to the preceding stage, then one falls into the error of degrading the profound into the shallow; how can this be avoided? Question:
If this is so, why does the Buddha call it the "expedient means of the initial mind"? Answer: I say that it is because the original intent of that [position] was not clearly understood.

Clarify this precisely at this juncture. It is only when one’s merit is perfected through this universal penetration (*pūrṇa-samantabhadrābhijñā*) that one first realizes the first of the fifty-five stages;
compared to the subsequent fifty-four stages, this constitutes the initial mind (*ādikarmika-citta*).

How could it be erroneously judged as the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) according to the preceding text, and thus designated as its "initial mind"? Furthermore, this initial mind corresponds distantly to the Sublime Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), serving as the ultimate culmination.
The Great Sūtra states: "The initial mind and the ultimate mind are not different; yet between these two minds, the former is more difficult.
Furthermore, because this first stage is called the "Stage of Resolving the Mind," the sūtra further states: "From the very first resolution of the mind, one attains perfect enlightenment.
If this is so, then this initial mind is by no means superficial. I maintain that it is a perfect penetration reaching all the way to the ultimate stage, and it is certainly not without vision.

Yet you say this. What kind of error is it to claim that the three contemplations (*sanguan*) come first and are thus profound, while the perfect penetration (*yuantong*) comes later and is thus shallow?

Is this not a grave loss of the proper sequence of depth and shallowness? I urge those who seek the Great Samādhi to investigate and refine the method of cultivation through the ear-door extensively, and to practice it with vigor.
Do not allow even a hair’s breadth of confusion to enter the three contemplations; only then will the Perfect [Samādhi]...

Only through such universal applicability can one hope for success. Question: The Great Master Zhiyi is the patriarch of this school, and the Three Contemplations (*sanguan*) are the practice of the Perfect and Sudden (*yuantun*).
Now you say that by relying on them, the entire scripture’s obstacles are exhausted; by practicing them, one must not err by even a hair’s breadth.

If this is so, does the contemplation established by Tiantai not accord with the principles of the Perfect and Sudden teaching? Please state which teaching it is subsumed under. Answer: This is yet another matter.
There are two points that are difficult for people to understand; they do not mean that the three contemplations are incompatible with the Perfect and Sudden teaching.

First, when the Buddha spoke of the inherent presence of the three [vehicles], he never established the three contemplations as such, yet commentators have erroneously cited the three contemplations to interpret them.
Failing to clarify this would allow cultivation to obstruct nature; therefore, it is necessary to distinguish between them. Second, there is the method of "hearing in reverse" (pratyāhāra).

Although one does not employ *vitarka* (initial application) and *vicāra* (sustained application), how could the three contemplations possibly be without them? If they were to be confused with these, it would necessitate the abandonment of "reverse-hearing" (*pratyāśravaṇa*);
therefore, they must be prohibited. These three contemplations are not inconsistent with the principles of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching;

however, they simply do not accord with the practice-gate of the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*. One should know that within each teaching, many dharma-gates are subsumed; thus, there is no [contradiction] among the dharma-gates.
[Question: How can one claim that the teachings are also different simply because the gates [of entry] are not the same? [Question:

Since both gates are equally the profound and sudden teaching (*yuanton jiao*), is there any distinction of superiority or inferiority between them? [Answer: You ask about Tiantai; how does he compare to the twenty-five sages? [The interlocutor replies:
"The Great Master would certainly not deceive himself. He himself said that he was only at the stage of the five ranks (*wupin*); how could he have suddenly equaled those great beings?
"Is it so, Holy One? [The Master] replied: "Mañjuśrī alone has selected the gate of the ear; thus, the gates of cultivation of the twenty-four sages cannot all be equalized.

How much less could they be equalized by the single gate of cultivation of Tiantai? Furthermore, the purports of the sutras and the purports of contemplation differ in many ways, yet the old commentaries have conflated them, never distinguishing right from wrong.
It is no wonder that they have used that to indiscriminately substitute for this. Now, I shall provide a brief [explanation].
An analysis reveals four points of difference. First, this sutra begins by refuting the *vijñāna-citta* (consciousness-mind), instructing that it be ultimately not employed. One wonders:
when Tiantai first expounded the Three Contemplations (*sanguan*), did he also first refute consciousness and teach its non-employment?

However, I have previously seen in the Tripitaka what is transmitted as the "Mind Seal" (*xin-yin*) of the Tiantai school, which first does not calculate or select away the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*), but rather [proceeds otherwise].
To seek the true mind [as you do] is in great contradiction with the intent of the sutra; this is the first point of difference.
Second, this sutra subsequently demonstrates that the essence of nature within the faculties is precisely the wondrously luminous true mind.

Do you not recognize that when Tiantai points to the true mind, he also says it is "nothing other than your six faculties"? Even if one were to take his established Three Truths, they would be roughly similar.
It resembles the Tripiṭaka, yet it points directly to the wind; initially, it does not recommend the six sense-faculties—this is the second difference.
